title: Danny Faure
text:
Danny Roland Faure was born on 13 May 1962 in Victoria, Mahé, Seychelles, the son of Roland Faure, a teacher and later a government official, and his wife, Marie-Antoinette Marguerite. His early education took place at the Victoria Primary School and then at the Seychelles College, a leading secondary school in the country, completing his studies there in 1980. Following his secondary education, Faure pursued tertiary studies, attending the University of East London in the United Kingdom, where he obtained a Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree in 1983. He then continued his legal training, qualifying as a barrister-at-law at the Council of Legal Education in London in 1985.

Returning to Seychelles, Faure began his professional career as a legal counsel in the Attorney General’s Office in 1986. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a State Counsel in 1988. During this period, he was involved in drafting legislation and advising the government on legal matters. His early career coincided with a period of political transition in the Seychelles, following the 1977 coup led by France-Albert René, which established a one-party socialist state. 

Faure’s direct involvement in politics began in 1993 when he was appointed as a Member of the National Assembly representing the Saint Louis constituency. He served continuously as a Member of Parliament for over two decades, until 2016.  He was a key figure within the Seychelles People’s Progressive Party (SPPP), the party founded by René, and played a significant role in the party’s political strategy and policy development.  In 1998, he was appointed as Minister for Education and Youth, a portfolio he held until 2005. During his time as Minister of Education, he oversaw significant reforms aimed at improving access to education and enhancing the quality of teaching. He championed initiatives to promote vocational training and skills development, reflecting a focus on equipping Seychellois youth with the skills needed for employment.

In 2005, President James Michel appointed Faure as Minister for Finance and Trade. This was a pivotal role, particularly given the economic challenges facing the Seychelles at the time, including a significant debt burden and vulnerability to external economic shocks.  He led negotiations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Paris Club of creditor nations to restructure the country’s debt. He oversaw the implementation of economic reforms, including fiscal consolidation measures, privatization of state-owned enterprises, and the introduction of a value-added tax (VAT) in 2011. These reforms were often controversial, but were presented as necessary to stabilize the economy and achieve sustainable growth. 

On 16 October 2016, in a surprise move, President James Michel announced his resignation and named Danny Faure as his successor. Faure was sworn in as the fourth President of Seychelles the same day, becoming the first president to assume office through a constitutional transfer of power rather than through an election or coup. He served the remainder of Michel's term and then sought a full five-year term in the 2018 presidential election. 

During his presidency, Faure prioritized good governance, transparency, and the fight against corruption. He initiated reforms to strengthen the rule of law and promote greater accountability in public administration. He also focused on environmental conservation, particularly protecting the Seychelles' marine biodiversity. He increased the area of marine protected areas significantly, committing to protect 30% of Seychelles’ Exclusive Economic Zone by 2020, a goal achieved ahead of schedule. He also launched initiatives to combat climate change and promote sustainable tourism. 

In the 2020 presidential election, Faure was defeated by Wavel Ramkalawan of the United Seychelles party (formerly the SPPP). He conceded defeat gracefully, marking the first peaceful transfer of power from one political party to another in Seychelles’ history. Since leaving office in October 2020, Faure has maintained a relatively low public profile, dedicating himself to private pursuits and occasionally speaking on issues related to governance and sustainable development. He remains a prominent figure in Seychellois politics, and continues to advocate for the continued progress and stability of his nation.

title: Joji (musician)
text:
George Kusunoki Miller, known professionally as Joji, was born on September 18, 1992, in Osaka, Japan. His father was an American father of Japanese and Native American descent, and his mother was Japanese. His early childhood was transient; he moved to Macao with his family at the age of two, and subsequently to Melbourne, Australia, when he was eleven in 2003. He attended high school at St Kevin’s College, a Catholic all-boys school in Toorak, Melbourne, graduating in 2012. It was during this period he began experimenting with music production, initially through GarageBand on his computer. He credits his early musical influences as being primarily R&B artists like Frank Ocean and also Japanese city pop.

Before rising to prominence as a solo artist, Miller gained initial recognition online primarily through comedic videos on YouTube under the alias Filthy Frank and his associated channel TVFilthyFrank, beginning around 2011.  These videos were characterized by surreal, often offensive, and deliberately low-budget humor, developing a dedicated, albeit controversial, cult following.  A core component of this online persona was the character Pink Guy, a hyper-masculine, pink-clad alter ego that rapidly became a meme.  Alongside this comedy work, he began uploading music to SoundCloud under the name Pink Season in 2015, offering a stark contrast to his comedic online persona. These early tracks, often lo-fi and melancholic, hinted at the musical direction he would later fully embrace.

In December 2017, Miller abruptly announced the retirement of both the Filthy Frank and Pink Guy characters, citing mental health concerns and the overwhelming nature of the online persona. He explained the performative aspect of the character had become detrimental to his well-being. This decision, though initially shocking to his fanbase, paved the way for him to focus solely on his music.

He officially adopted the stage name Joji and released his debut single, “Winter Strikes,” in March 2018. The song quickly gained traction, amassing over a million plays on Spotify within a month. He followed this with the EP *XXXtentacion* (not affiliated with the rapper of the same name) in September 2018, which further solidified his sound – a blend of lo-fi hip hop, R&B, and ambient electronic music, often characterized by themes of loneliness, heartbreak, and existentialism. The EP peaked at number 31 on the Billboard 200 chart.

Joji's breakthrough came with the single “Slow Dancing in the Dark,” released in October 2018.  The song went viral, driven largely by its emotional resonance and relatable lyrics, and was certified Platinum by the RIAA in December 2020.  He released his debut studio album, *Ballads 1*, in October 2018, which reached number 3 on the Billboard 200 and received generally positive reviews. The album showcased a refined, more polished version of the sound established in his earlier work. 

In 2020, Joji released his second studio album, *Nectar*, in September.  The album featured collaborations with artists like Diplo, Yves V, and Omar Apollo. *Nectar* debuted at number 3 on the Billboard 200, becoming his highest-charting album to date. He supported the album with a planned world tour in 2021, which was significantly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

His third studio album, *Smithereens*, was released in October 2022.  It marked a slight shift in sound, incorporating more experimental and darker elements. While not reaching the commercial heights of *Nectar*, it was critically well-received and demonstrated his continued artistic exploration.  

As of late 2023, Joji continues to release music and perform live. He has earned multiple Platinum certifications for his singles and albums.  He maintains a relatively private personal life, rarely granting interviews and largely letting his music speak for itself.  He is currently signed to 88rising, an Asian-American music collective, and remains a significant figure in the contemporary alternative R&B and lo-fi music scenes, with over 14 million monthly listeners on Spotify as of November 2023.

title: Marty Mayberry
text:
Marty Mayberry, born Martin Lee Mayberry on October 26, 1956, in Benton, Illinois, is a retired American professional rodeo cowboy who specialized in bull riding. His career spanned nearly two decades and culminated in a world championship, solidifying his place as a legend in the sport. He was the son of Gene and Betty Mayberry, and grew up on a family farm where he began riding horses at a very young age. This early exposure to livestock and rural life proved crucial in developing the skills and tenacity needed for a career in rodeo. 

Mayberry’s interest in bull riding began in his teenage years, initially competing in local rodeos and high school events around Southern Illinois. He quickly excelled, demonstrating a natural aptitude for the sport and an unusually calm demeanor for someone facing a 2,000-pound animal. After graduating from Benton High School in 1974, he bypassed traditional college plans, opting instead to pursue rodeo full-time. He initially traveled the circuit independently, relying on winnings and the support of his family. 

His professional rodeo career officially began in 1975 with the Rodeo Cowboys Association (RCA), which would later become the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association (PRCA). The early years were characterized by consistent, though not spectacular, performance. He steadily climbed the rankings, earning enough to sustain his lifestyle but lacking the breakthrough wins needed to become a top contender. He spent considerable time honing his technique, working with experienced bull riders and learning from both successes and failures. 

The turning point came in the late 1980s. Mayberry’s dedication and refined skills began to translate into significant victories. In 1987, he finished 8th in the world standings, a considerable improvement. 1989 was his banner year. He won the National Finals Rodeo (NFR) in Las Vegas, Nevada, with an impressive cumulative score of 438 points on 10 bulls. This win, combined with consistent performance throughout the year, earned him the 1989 PRCA World Championship in Bull Riding. He earned $128,793 in that championship year, a substantial amount at the time. Throughout his career, he consistently rode for renowned stock contractors like Beutler & Son and Frontier Rodeo, often drawing some of the most challenging bulls in the business.

Mayberry was known for his smooth, balanced style and his ability to “stay centered” on the bull, absorbing the animal’s movements. He wasn’t a flashy rider known for high-risk maneuvers, but rather one who focused on consistency and control. He was also respected for his sportsmanship and calm demeanor, even in the face of danger. This earned him the admiration of fellow competitors and fans alike. 

He continued to compete at a high level through the early 1990s, though injuries began to take their toll. He suffered numerous concussions and broken bones, typical consequences of a bull riding career. He officially retired from professional rodeo in 1994 at the age of 37, acknowledging the physical demands and the need to protect his long-term health.

Following his retirement, Mayberry remained involved in the rodeo world, though in a less physically demanding capacity. He spent several years working as a stock contractor, providing bulls for rodeo events. He also became a popular rodeo clinician, sharing his knowledge and experience with aspiring bull riders.  He moved back to his hometown of Benton, Illinois, and remained active in the local community. 



In 2018, Marty Mayberry was inducted into the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum’s Rodeo Hall of Fame in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, further cementing his legacy as one of the great bull riders of his era. As of late 2023, Mayberry resides in Illinois and enjoys spending time with his family. He is considered a quiet, humble icon of the sport, remembered not only for his championship but also for his grace and dedication to the cowboy way of life.

title: Raúl Esparza
text:
Raúl Eduardo Esparza was born on March 30, 1970, in Hartford, Connecticut, to Cuban parents, Roberto Esparza and Lourdes Esparza. His father was a poet and his mother a classically trained singer, fostering a creative environment from a young age. The family moved to Mission, Texas, in the Rio Grande Valley, when Raúl was four years old, a transition that significantly shaped his identity. He frequently speaks of the cultural richness and complexities of growing up near the border, navigating both American and Mexican cultures. He has described his childhood as somewhat nomadic, moving frequently within the Rio Grande Valley due to his father’s work as a migrant worker advocate. 

Esparza’s early education included attending Sharyland High School in Sharyland, Texas, where he participated in the debate team and discovered a talent for performance. He initially planned to pursue a career in political science, and in 1988, he enrolled at Harvard University, intending to become a lawyer. However, he found himself increasingly drawn to the university’s theater scene. He became heavily involved with the American Repertory Theater, performing in numerous productions and eventually changing his major to English and American Literature. He graduated from Harvard in 1992 with a Bachelor of Arts degree.

Following graduation, Esparza initially pursued a career in advertising in New York City, working at the agency Margeotes Fertitta & Partners. However, his passion for acting proved too strong. He began taking acting classes and performing in off-Broadway productions. His Broadway debut came in 1995 as a replacement in the musical *Aspects of Love*. This was followed by roles in *The Importance of Being Earnest* (1996) and *Romeo and Juliet* (1996) at the Roundabout Theatre Company.

A major breakthrough came in 2000 when he originated the role of Sidney Brustein in the Broadway revival of Lorraine Hansberry’s *The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window*, earning him his first Tony Award nomination for Best Featured Actor in a Play. He continued to gain recognition with roles in *Company* (2000) and *Cabaret* (2001), showcasing his versatility. 

Esparza’s most celebrated role to date is arguably as Emmet Forrest in John Kander and Greg Pierce’s musical *Chicago*, which he joined in 2005. He received a Tony Award nomination for Best Actor in a Musical in 2006 and continued with the production for over a year, becoming a popular and critically acclaimed Billy Flynn. He reprised the role multiple times in subsequent years, including a 2017 return engagement. 

Beyond stage work, Esparza has built a substantial television career. He is perhaps best known for his role as Rafael Santana on the NBC legal drama *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit*, appearing in 88 episodes between 2011 and 2017. He also had recurring roles on *Hannibal* (2013-2015) and *Once Upon a Time* (2018). He’s made guest appearances on numerous other television shows, including *Six Feet Under*, *Rescue Me*, and *The Good Wife*.

In 2014, Esparza received a Special Tony Award for Lifetime Excellence in the Theatre. He is a dedicated advocate for arts education and has actively worked with organizations promoting accessibility to the performing arts. He has also been a vocal advocate for immigration rights, drawing on his own experiences growing up in a border community. 

Currently, Esparza continues to work in theatre, film, and television. He resides in New York City with his partner, architect David Neuhauser, and their son. He has remained consistently active in the performing arts, demonstrating a career spanning over three decades and solidifying his position as a highly respected and versatile actor.

title: Aditya Kalyanpur
text:
Aditya Kalyanpur was born on December 16, 1948, in Mumbai, India, to a family deeply rooted in journalism. His father, Vimla Kalyanpur, was a pioneering female journalist in India, working with the *Hindustan Times* and becoming the first female editor of a major Indian newspaper. This environment profoundly shaped Kalyanpur’s own life and career path. He received his early education at the Campion School, a Jesuit-run institution in Mumbai, and then attended St. Xavier's College, also in Mumbai, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics and Politics in 1970. He furthered his education at the University of California, Berkeley, earning a Master of Arts degree in Journalism in 1972. 

Kalyanpur began his journalistic career at the *Free Press Journal* in Mumbai in 1973, starting as a reporter covering labor and political issues. He quickly demonstrated a talent for investigative reporting, and within two years, rose to become the paper’s Assistant Editor.  A significant turning point came in 1975 during the Emergency declared by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Kalyanpur, along with other journalists, faced considerable pressure from the government for independent reporting. He was briefly detained under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) in 1976, a period lasting approximately three months, for his critical coverage of the government. This experience solidified his commitment to press freedom and fearless journalism.

In 1980, Kalyanpur moved to Delhi and joined *India Today* magazine, which was then rapidly becoming a leading news publication. He initially served as a Senior Editor, focusing on political and economic affairs.  His sharp analysis and in-depth reporting quickly made him a prominent voice in Indian journalism. He was instrumental in establishing *India Today's* reputation for investigative journalism, leading teams that uncovered stories on corruption, political intrigue, and social issues.  He was promoted to Executive Editor in 1986 and then to Deputy Editor in 1990. 

A defining moment in Kalyanpur’s career came with the Rajiv Gandhi assassination in 1991. *India Today* assigned him to lead a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the assassination and the alleged lapses in security. The resulting coverage, published as a special issue and later compiled into a book titled *The Rajiv Gandhi Assassination: The Investigation*, was widely acclaimed for its meticulous detail and insightful analysis. The book, published in 1992, became a bestseller and is still considered a definitive account of the event. He also received the prestigious Prem Bhatia Award for journalistic excellence in 1992 for his work on the assassination investigation. 

Kalyanpur continued to work at *India Today* through the 1990s, covering the political and economic upheavals in India, including the liberalization policies initiated in 1991. He played a crucial role in expanding the magazine’s coverage of international affairs and strengthening its investigative reporting capabilities. In 2000, he left *India Today* and became a consulting editor for *The Pioneer*, a national English-language daily.  

In 2004, Kalyanpur co-founded the Centre for Investigative Journalism (CIJ) in New Delhi, an independent non-profit organization dedicated to promoting investigative journalism in India. He served as the Director of the CIJ until 2013, mentoring young journalists and supporting in-depth investigations on critical issues. He also authored a second book, *The Political Economy of India*, published in 2010, analyzing the dynamics of economic growth and political power in India.

Aditya Kalyanpur remained active in journalism and public discourse throughout his later life, frequently contributing opinion pieces and analyses to various publications. He was a vocal advocate for press freedom and ethical journalism. He passed away on November 16, 2023, in New Delhi, at the age of 74, leaving behind a legacy as one of India’s most respected and influential journalists. He is survived by his wife, Shalini Kalyanpur, and their son, Rohan Kalyanpur.

title: Lionel Messi
text:
Lionel Andrés Messi Cuccittini was born on June 24, 1987, in Rosario, Argentina, the third of four children to Jorge Messi, a steel factory manager, and Celia María Cuccittini, a part-time cleaner. His siblings are Rodrigo, Matías, and María Sol. From a young age, Messi displayed a prodigious talent for football, playing for Grandoli, a local club coached by his father, and later for Newell’s Old Boys, one of Rosario’s most prominent clubs. However, at age 11, Messi was diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency, a condition requiring expensive medical treatment. Newell's Old Boys promised to contribute to the costs, but later reneged, and River Plate, another Argentine powerhouse, showed interest but also hesitated due to the financial burden. 

In September 2000, at the age of 13, Messi and his father travelled to Barcelona, Spain, for a trial with FC Barcelona. Carles Rexach, the club’s sporting director, was immediately impressed, famously offering Messi a contract written on a paper napkin. Barcelona agreed to pay for Messi’s medical treatment, and he joined their youth academy, La Masia. He quickly progressed through the ranks, playing in various youth teams. He was initially homesick and struggled to adapt to life away from his family, but his talent shone through.

Messi made his official debut for Barcelona’s first team on November 16, 2003, in a friendly match against Porto. His La Liga debut followed on October 16, 2004, against Espanyol. While initially a substitute player, his skill and dribbling ability became increasingly apparent. The 2005-06 season saw a breakthrough, as he scored six league goals and helped Barcelona win La Liga and the Champions League. 

Over the next decade and a half, Messi became the focal point of Barcelona’s success. He won ten La Liga titles (2005-06, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2012-13, 2014-15, 2015-16, 2017-18, 2018-19, 2020-21), seven Copa del Rey titles (2008-09, 2011-12, 2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2020-21) and four Champions League titles (2005-06, 2008-09, 2010-11, 2014-15). Individually, he achieved unprecedented success. He won the Ballon d’Or – awarded to the world’s best player – a record eight times (2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2019, 2021, 2023). He also holds the record for most goals scored in La Liga (474) and most goals scored for a single club (672 for Barcelona).

For the Argentina national team, Messi's career initially lacked the same level of success. He participated in the 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, reaching the final in 2014, where Argentina lost to Germany. He also featured in several Copa América tournaments, suffering defeats in the finals in 2007, 2015 and 2016, leading to considerable criticism from fans and media. However, he finally broke this drought by captaining Argentina to victory in the 2021 Copa América, defeating Brazil 1-0 in the final at the Maracanã Stadium. 

His long-awaited World Cup triumph came in December 2022, when he led Argentina to victory over France in a thrilling penalty shootout in the final held in Doha, Qatar. Messi scored twice in the match and was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player. He currently holds the record for most appearances (180) and goals (106) for Argentina.

In August 2021, due to Barcelona's financial difficulties, Messi left the club after 21 years, signing for Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) on a two-year contract. He won two Ligue 1 titles with PSG (2021-22, 2022-23) before joining Inter Miami of Major League Soccer (MLS) in July 2023. He instantly impacted the league, leading Inter Miami to victory in the Leagues Cup in August 2023. 

Messi married Antonela Roccuzzo, his childhood sweetheart, in Rosario on June 30, 2017. They have three sons: Thiago, Mateo, and Ciro. He continues to be a global icon, admired for his exceptional footballing ability, humility, and dedication to the sport.

title: Leo Kokubo
text:
Leo Kokubo was born on November 17, 1916, in Seattle, Washington, to Japanese immigrant parents, Kenzo and Kiyo Kokubo. His father was a fisherman and his mother managed a boarding house for other Japanese fishermen. Kokubo’s early life was steeped in the close-knit Japanese-American community of Seattle’s International District, then known as Nihonmachi. He attended Beacon Hill Elementary School and later Garfield High School, graduating in 1934. Even as a child, Kokubo displayed a talent for art, initially sketching and painting scenes of the Puget Sound and the fishing boats his father worked on. He received early artistic training from local artists, including George Tsutakawa, who would become a renowned sculptor himself.

Kokubo initially pursued a practical career path, enrolling at the University of Washington in 1934 to study architecture, influenced by his father's desire for him to have a stable profession. However, his passion for art proved stronger. He left the university after a year to dedicate himself to painting, studying briefly at the Art Instruction Schools in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 1935.  Returning to Seattle, he worked as a commercial artist, undertaking commissions for advertising and illustrations while continuing to develop his personal artistic style. 

The outbreak of World War II dramatically altered Kokubo’s life, as it did for all Japanese Americans. Following Executive Order 9066 in 1942, he and his family were forcibly removed from their home and incarcerated at the Minidoka Relocation Center in Idaho.  Despite the hardship and injustice, Kokubo continued to paint within the camp, documenting life inside the barbed-wire enclosures and the surrounding landscape. He became a key figure in establishing an art school within Minidoka, teaching art to fellow internees, including children, providing a vital creative outlet during a period of immense trauma. He also served as a camp newspaper illustrator.

After the war’s end in 1945, Kokubo and his family returned to Seattle. He resumed his artistic career, initially focusing on watercolor landscapes of the Pacific Northwest. He quickly gained recognition for his realistic depictions of the region’s natural beauty, particularly his scenes of Mount Rainier, Puget Sound, and the San Juan Islands. In 1947, he became a founding member of the Northwest Watercolor Society, later serving as its president from 1953 to 1955. 

Kokubo’s style evolved over the decades, incorporating elements of abstraction while maintaining his commitment to representational form. He experimented with acrylics and mixed media, often using collage elements. He was influenced by the American Impressionists and the Northwest School of artists, but developed a distinct voice characterized by luminous color and atmospheric effects.  He held numerous solo exhibitions throughout his career, including shows at the Seattle Art Museum (1964, 1983) and the Portland Art Museum (1972).  He received several awards, including the Seattle Arts Commission’s Award for Excellence in 1973 and a National Endowment for the Arts grant in 1981. 

Kokubo also dedicated significant time to teaching. He taught watercolor painting at the Seattle Art Museum from 1951 to 1985, impacting generations of artists. He also taught at the University of Washington Extension and privately mentored numerous students. He was known for his patient and encouraging teaching style.

In his later life, Kokubo became increasingly involved in addressing the legacy of the Japanese American internment. He actively participated in redress efforts and spoke publicly about his experiences during the war. His wartime paintings from Minidoka became particularly significant, serving as powerful visual documents of a dark chapter in American history. 

Leo Kokubo died on November 29, 2002, in Seattle, at the age of 86.  His artwork is held in numerous public and private collections, including the Seattle Art Museum, the Washington State Historical Society, and the Portland Art Museum. He is remembered not only as a talented artist but also as a resilient and compassionate individual who used his art to document his experiences and to connect with others.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Christina Arterton was born on February 2, 1986, in Gravesend, Kent, England. Her mother, Sally-Anne, worked as a mobile hairdresser, and her father, Shahid John Arterton, was a designer. Her ancestry is diverse; her father was of Pakistani descent and her mother is English. Arterton grew up in a council house in Northfleet, a relatively deprived area, and attended Northfleet Technology College. She described her childhood as happy but acknowledged the financial struggles her family faced. She displayed a passion for performing arts from a young age, joining the local youth theatre group, the Northfleet Players, at the age of eight. She continued her training with the National Youth Theatre, attending workshops during school holidays.  

Arterton initially intended to study fashion at the University of Central Lancashire, but changed her mind and pursued acting. She earned a scholarship to the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London in 2005, graduating in 2008. While at RADA, she supplemented her income with jobs including working as a hostess at a Five Guys burger restaurant.  It was during her final year at RADA that her professional career began to take shape.

Her breakthrough role came in 2008 with the Bond film *Quantum of Solace*, where she played Strawberry Fields, a Bond girl. Though the role was relatively small, it brought her significant public attention.  Almost immediately following, she starred in Guy Ritchie’s *RocknRolla* (also 2008), demonstrating a versatility beyond the glamorous Bond persona.  2009 proved to be a pivotal year. She landed the lead in *Bright Star*, Jane Campion’s biographical romance about the poet John Keats and Fanny Brawne, garnering critical acclaim for her performance. She also appeared in *Clash of the Titans* (2010), a big-budget fantasy epic, further expanding her profile. 

The early 2010s saw Arterton solidify her position as a leading British actress. She starred in *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* (2010), *Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters* (2013), and *Byzantium* (2013), a vampire drama directed by Neil Jordan which saw her reunited with *Bright Star* co-star Ben Whishaw.  She also began to showcase her stage talents, making her West End debut in 2013 as Zaida in Jez Butterworth’s *The River*, receiving positive reviews. 

Arterton actively sought roles that challenged her and moved away from stereotypical “glamour girl” portrayals.  She took on independent projects like *Their Finest* (2016), a critically acclaimed wartime drama where she played Catrin Cole, a screenwriter, and *Vita and Virginia* (2018), in which she portrayed Virginia Woolf. In 2019, she starred in the lead role of Tess in the BBC Two miniseries *Summer of Rockets*, a Cold War espionage thriller. 

Throughout her career, Arterton has also maintained a strong commitment to theatre. She has appeared in productions of *The Duchess of Malfi* (2014) at the Shakespeare’s Globe, earning praise for her performance, and *Saint Joan* (2017) at the Donmar Warehouse. In 2023, she starred in the play *Waste* at the National Theatre.

Arterton married Rory Keenan, an Irish actor, in 2015. They have one daughter, born in December 2018. She has become increasingly vocal on issues surrounding the representation of women in film and the need for greater diversity within the industry. In 2016 she spoke out about the pressure she felt to conform to certain physical expectations in Hollywood and her decision to step back from overtly sexualized roles.  She continues to work consistently in film, television, and theatre, balancing commercial projects with more independent and artistically driven work.  As of late 2023, she resides in London with her family and remains a prominent figure in the British acting scene.

title: Sofiane Feghouli
text:
Sofiane Feghouli was born on September 1, 1989, in Trappes, a commune in the Yvelines département in the Île-de-France region of France, to Algerian parents. His family had immigrated to France from Algeria in the 1980s. Growing up in the working-class suburbs of Paris, Feghouli displayed a natural talent for football from a young age, honing his skills on the local streets and pitches. He began his formal footballing journey at the age of eight, joining the youth academy of US Trappes. He spent six years there, quickly standing out as a gifted and technically proficient player.

Recognized for his potential, Feghouli was scouted by several professional clubs and ultimately joined Grenoble Foot 38 in 2003, at the age of 14. He progressed through their youth system, and on September 21, 2007, he made his professional debut for Grenoble in a Ligue 2 match against Bastia. He was 18 years old at the time. Over the next two seasons, Feghouli became a regular starter for Grenoble, demonstrating his dribbling ability, vision, and capacity to contribute goals. He played in 36 league games over those two seasons, scoring 7 goals.

His performances attracted the attention of larger clubs, and in June 2009, he signed for Valenciennes FC for a reported fee of €3 million. At Valenciennes, Feghouli continued to develop as a player, flourishing in a more attacking role. He played 75 league matches for the club, scoring 12 goals and establishing himself as one of the most promising young talents in Ligue 1. 

In May 2013, Feghouli made a significant move to Valencia CF in Spain, joining on a free transfer after his contract with Valenciennes expired. He quickly became a key player for Valencia, showcasing his versatility and ability to play in multiple attacking positions. During his four seasons with the club, he made 130 appearances across all competitions, scoring 30 goals. He became a fan favourite at the Mestalla Stadium, known for his skillful play and dedication. His peak form at Valencia saw him considered one of the league's most exciting players. 

In August 2016, Feghouli joined West Ham United in the English Premier League on a free transfer. His time at West Ham was less impactful than his previous clubs. He struggled to consistently find his form and adapt to the physicality of the Premier League. He played 32 games for the Hammers, scoring 4 goals, before being released in July 2018.

Following his departure from West Ham, Feghouli returned to Galatasaray in Turkey, signing a two-year contract in August 2018. He found success again, becoming an integral part of the Galatasaray squad. He won the Süper Lig title with Galatasaray in the 2018-19 season, contributing significantly with 8 goals and 8 assists. He continued to be a key player for the club, playing over 100 games and winning another league title in the 2020-21 season. 

Internationally, Feghouli was eligible to represent both France and Algeria. He initially represented France at various youth levels, including the Under-21 team. However, he ultimately chose to represent Algeria, making his debut for the national team on March 26, 2012, in a friendly match against Egypt. He became a crucial member of the Algerian national team, playing in the 2013, 2015, 2017 and 2019 Africa Cup of Nations tournaments. He was a key figure in Algeria’s successful 2019 Africa Cup of Nations campaign, where they won the tournament, defeating Senegal in the final. Feghouli played in all seven matches of the tournament. He announced his retirement from international football on March 29, 2021, having earned 51 caps for Algeria and scoring 7 goals.

As of late 2023, Feghouli continues to play professional football, returning to his first club, US Trappes, in December 2023 at the age of 34, aiming to help the club progress through the French regional leagues. This marked a return to his roots and a gesture of giving back to the community where his footballing journey began.

title: Melvin Van Peebles
text:
Melvin Van Peebles, born Melvin Purvis Peebles on August 22, 1932, in Chicago, Illinois, was a pioneering African-American filmmaker, actor, and musician who fundamentally altered the landscape of American cinema. His early life was marked by a diverse educational and geographical journey. His mother, Augustama, was a seamstress, and his father, Robert Peebles, was a Pullman porter. He attended DuSable High School in Chicago, a historically Black high school known for producing accomplished alumni. Following high school, Van Peebles briefly attended West Virginia State University before transferring to Ohio Wesleyan University, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in English in 1954. He then served in the United States Air Force from 1954 to 1957, stationed in France, where he also developed a passion for painting and began writing. 

Following his military service, Van Peebles moved to Mexico City in 1958 and then to Paris in 1959, immersing himself in the European art scene. He worked as a journalist, painter, and street performer, even appearing in French theater productions. He also began writing novels, publishing “The Big Four” in 1963, followed by “Les Aventuriers” (The Adventurers) in 1964, which became a bestseller in France and was adapted into a 1967 film starring Burt Lancaster, though Van Peebles had little creative control over the adaptation.

Returning to the United States in 1968, Van Peebles dedicated himself to filmmaking, motivated by a desire to create stories that reflected the Black experience authentically and challenged existing Hollywood norms. He founded Melvin Van Peebles Productions and secured funding—a relatively small $50,000—to produce his groundbreaking film, *Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song* (1971).  Shot in just 19 days in the Mojave Desert, the film was a defiant response to the Blaxploitation genre that was beginning to emerge, but aimed to be more politically charged and stylistically innovative.  *Sweet Sweetback* deliberately eschewed conventional narrative structure, employing fragmented scenes, poetic dialogue, and a focus on Black male empowerment. Though controversial, the film grossed over $15 million and became a cult classic, influencing a generation of Black filmmakers.

The success of *Sweet Sweetback* allowed Van Peebles to continue making films, though with varying degrees of commercial success. He directed *Watermelon Man* (1972), a satirical comedy about a white insurance investigator who inexplicably turns Black, which earned him a Writers Guild of America Award nomination.  He followed with *Posse* (1973), a Western featuring an all-Black cast.  Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Van Peebles continued to direct, write, and occasionally act in films, including *Greased Lightning* (1977) and *Identity Crisis* (1989). He also worked in theater, directing and choreographing productions on and off Broadway.

His son, Mario Van Peebles, followed in his footsteps, becoming a successful actor and director in his own right. They collaborated on several projects, including the 1992 film *Posse*, a remake of Melvin's 1973 film, and the HBO series *Baadasssss!* which chronicled Melvin's life and career. 

In his later life, Van Peebles remained a vocal advocate for independent filmmaking and Black representation in the arts. He received an Honorary Palme d'Or at the 2021 Cannes Film Festival, recognizing his lifetime achievement.  In September 2021, shortly before his death, the American Film Institute presented him with the AFI Life Achievement Award, recognizing his outstanding contributions to the art of motion pictures.  Melvin Van Peebles died on September 24, 2021, in New York City, at the age of 89, leaving behind a legacy as a fearless innovator and a crucial figure in the history of American cinema. He is survived by his three children: Mario, Dedra and Robin.

title: Ivan Toms
text:
Ivan Toms was born on 21st July 1951 in Lusaka, Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia), to South African parents in exile. His parents, Fred and Sylvia Toms, were both anti-apartheid activists and members of the South African Communist Party (SACP). They fled South Africa in 1960 following increasing repression and were involved in providing logistical support to Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the African National Congress (ANC). Ivan spent his formative years in Zambia, attending Lusaka’s Northmead School, and was deeply influenced by the political climate and the presence of numerous exiled South Africans. He became politically aware at a young age, assisting his parents with tasks related to the liberation struggle, including distributing pamphlets and occasionally acting as a courier.

In 1969, at the age of 18, Toms returned to South Africa illegally, driven by a desire to actively participate in the fight against apartheid. He initially joined the ANC’s underground network in the Witwatersrand area, operating under the name ‘David Motau’. He underwent military training in Botswana in 1972, and later in Angola, specializing in urban guerilla warfare and explosives. He rose through the ranks of Umkhonto we Sizwe, becoming a regional commander responsible for operations in the Johannesburg area. 

Between 1976 and 1985, Toms was central to a series of significant sabotage operations targeting economic and government infrastructure. He was involved in the bombing of the Wonderboom railway lines near Pretoria in 1976, the Ellis Park stadium bombing in 1980, and the sabotage of the Koösfontein gold refinery in 1980, an operation intended to disrupt the South African economy. He also played a key role in the 1982 bombing of the Air Force headquarters in Pretoria, which resulted in the death of 13 people and injury to 217. While he did not personally plant the bomb, he was a key strategist and coordinator. 

Arrested in 1985 following a raid on an ANC safe house in Johannesburg, Toms was charged with sabotage and murder related to the Air Force headquarters bombing. The trial, which began in 1986, became a landmark case, attracting international attention. He refused legal representation, choosing instead to use the court as a platform to articulate the political motivations behind the ANC’s armed struggle and to denounce apartheid. He delivered a lengthy statement to the court, outlining the injustices of the system and justifying the use of violence as a last resort. In 1988, he was convicted on multiple counts, including sabotage and murder, and sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Toms served his sentence in Pollsmoor and later Diepkloof Maximum Security Prison. While incarcerated, he continued to be a symbol of resistance and engaged in political discussions with fellow prisoners and visiting officials.  He began to publicly question the continued use of armed struggle as South Africa moved towards negotiations.  He initiated a dialogue with prison authorities, advocating for improved conditions and greater political freedoms for prisoners.

Following the unbanning of the ANC in February 1990 and the release of Nelson Mandela, Toms was released from prison on 24th May 1991 as part of a general amnesty for political prisoners. He subsequently testified before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) in 1996, providing a detailed account of his involvement in Umkhonto we Sizwe operations. He sought amnesty for his actions, acknowledging the loss of life caused by the bombings but maintaining that they were undertaken in the context of a brutal and oppressive regime.  His amnesty was granted in 1998, though not without controversy given the scale of the violence he admitted to.

After his release, Toms dedicated himself to reconciliation and social justice. He worked as a consultant for the National Institute for Crime Prevention and Reintegration of Offenders (NICRO), focusing on restorative justice programs and reintegrating former political prisoners into society. He became a vocal advocate for demilitarization and the responsible use of force.  He authored his autobiography, “Holding My Enemy,” published in 2009, detailing his life in the struggle and his eventual embrace of reconciliation. Ivan Toms died on 18th February 2024 in Johannesburg, aged 72, leaving behind a complex legacy as a former freedom fighter who ultimately championed peace and forgiveness.

title: Shane Fontayne
text:
Shane Fontayne was born Shane Michael Fontayne on February 28, 1973, in Melbourne, Australia. His father, Bruce Fontayne, was a highly respected session musician, playing guitar for numerous Australian artists including John Farnham and Kylie Minogue, and his mother, Lynette, was a professional singer. This musical upbringing heavily influenced Fontayne’s early development; he began learning piano at the age of five, switching to guitar by age eight. He attended high school at Camberwell High School in Melbourne, but music quickly became his primary focus, leading him to leave school before completing his final year.

Fontayne’s professional music career began in the early 1990s, initially playing in various cover bands around Melbourne’s pub and club circuit. He quickly gained a reputation as a versatile and technically proficient guitarist. In 1994, he joined the band Pearly, fronted by singer-songwriter Rebecca Barnard. Pearly released two albums, *Corner Store* in 1996 and *Supernatural* in 1998, achieving moderate success on the Australian alternative rock scene. Fontayne’s guitar work was integral to Pearly's sound, showcasing a blend of rock, blues, and country influences. 

A significant turning point came in 1999 when Fontayne joined the band Powderfinger. He replaced original guitarist Darren Middleton, who departed to focus on his own solo work. Powderfinger, already established as one of Australia’s most successful rock acts, had released three albums prior to Fontayne’s arrival. He debuted on their fourth studio album, *Odyssey Number Five* released in 2000, which achieved double platinum certification in Australia within weeks of its release. This album, and the subsequent tours, cemented Fontayne’s position as a prominent figure in Australian rock music.

Throughout his 18-year tenure with Powderfinger, Fontayne contributed significantly to the band’s songwriting and arrangements, alongside members Bernard Fanning, John Collins, Ian Haug, and Darin Osborne. He co-wrote several well-known tracks, including "Like a Dog" and "Free," both featured on the 2003 album *Vulture Street*, which debuted at number one on the ARIA charts and went on to achieve six times platinum status. Powderfinger continued to release commercially and critically acclaimed albums under Fontayne’s contribution, including *Dream Days at the Hotel Existence* (2007) and *Golden Rule* (2009), both reaching number one on the Australian album charts. The band won multiple ARIA Awards during this period, including Best Rock Album in 2004 for *Vulture Street* and again in 2007 for *Dream Days at the Hotel Existence*.

Fontayne's guitar style is characterized by its clarity, melodic sensibility, and his ability to seamlessly blend different genres. He is known for his use of both Fender and Gibson guitars, often employing a combination of clean and overdriven tones. He was consistently recognized as one of Australia's leading guitarists, appearing in numerous “best guitarist” polls in magazines like *Guitar Australia*.

In November 2010, Fontayne announced his departure from Powderfinger, citing a desire to explore other musical avenues and spend more time with his family. The band went on hiatus shortly after. Following his exit, Fontayne focused on session work, production, and his own solo projects. He collaborated with various artists, including Tim Rogers and Katie Noonan, and established himself as a sought-after producer at his private studio in Melbourne.

In 2016, Fontayne formed the band The Black Armada, releasing their debut album *Songs to Hum and Die To* in 2017. The album showcased a darker, more experimental side to his songwriting and guitar playing. He continues to work as a session musician, producer, and songwriter, maintaining a relatively low profile compared to his time with Powderfinger. He is married and has two children. While not actively touring extensively, Fontayne remains involved in the Australian music scene, occasionally performing at select events and continuing to contribute his talents to a diverse range of projects.

title: Iggy Azalea
text:
Amethyst Amelia Kelly, known professionally as Iggy Azalea, was born on June 7, 1990, in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. Her upbringing was unconventional. Her father, Brendan Kelly, was a painter and sculptor, while her mother, Tania, raised her largely alone in Mullumbimby, a small town in northern New South Wales. Azalea described her childhood as transient, moving frequently and experiencing a somewhat isolated existence. She didn’t attend traditional high school, instead completing her education via distance education, allowing her more time to focus on her burgeoning interest in music. Her early influences were heavily rooted in American hip-hop and pop culture, particularly artists like Tupac Shakur, Missy Elliott, and Salt-N-Pepa, despite growing up in a largely Australian environment. She began writing rap lyrics as a teenager, inspired by the lyrical complexity and storytelling she admired in American artists.

Azalea started sharing her music online around 2006, uploading songs and music videos to platforms like Myspace and YouTube. This self-promotion caught the attention of American producer Hype Williams, who featured her in a 2010 music video for his artist Travis McCoy. This marked her first significant exposure to a wider audience. Shortly after, in 2010, she relocated to the United States, initially living in Miami before settling in Los Angeles to pursue her music career more aggressively. 

Her initial American releases included the mixtapes *Ignoramus* (2011) and *TrapGold* (2012). *TrapGold* was particularly successful, generating buzz within the hip-hop community and attracting the attention of T.I., the Atlanta-based rapper and record executive. In 2013, Azalea signed with T.I.’s Grand Hustle imprint, alongside Atlantic Records. This partnership proved pivotal.

Her breakthrough came with the release of her debut studio album, *The New Classic*, on October 22, 2013. The album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart, selling 135,000 copies in its first week. It was the first female rapper to achieve this since Nicki Minaj in 2010. The album spawned the hit singles "Work," featuring A$AP Rocky, which peaked at number 63 on the Billboard Hot 100, and "Fancy," featuring Charli XCX, which became her signature song. "Fancy" topped the Billboard Hot 100 for seven weeks in 2014, making Azalea the first woman to reach the top of the chart as a solo artist since Lauryn Hill in 1998. *The New Classic* was eventually certified platinum by the RIAA.

Following the success of her debut, Azalea released her second studio album, *Digital Distortion*, in January 2016. While it debuted at number four on the Billboard 200, it didn’t achieve the same level of commercial success as *The New Classic*, despite singles like “Team” and “Beg For It.” The album's release was also delayed multiple times due to leaks and artist dissatisfaction.

In the years following *Digital Distortion*, Azalea faced criticism regarding cultural appropriation and her lyrical content. She also experienced personal challenges, including a highly publicized breakup with basketball player Nick Young in 2016.  She continued to release music, including the EP *Wicked Lips* in 2019, and the album *In My Defense* in 2019, which reached number 7 on the Billboard 200. 

In 2022, she released the album *The End of an Era*, marking what she described as the conclusion of her album-making era. She has since focused on singles and exploring different creative avenues, including a foray into reality television as a judge on the Australian singing competition *The X Factor Australia* in 2023.  Azalea and boyfriend Playboi Carti welcomed a son, Onyx Kelly, in April 2020. As of late 2023, she continues to tour and release music, maintaining a dedicated fanbase despite navigating a complex and often controversial career. Her net worth is estimated to be around $60 million as of 2023.

title: Rigoberto Torres
text:
Rigoberto Torres, a pivotal figure in the development of Dominican merengue music, was born on April 27, 1928, in Monte Cristi, a northern coastal city in the Dominican Republic. His parents, Rafael Torres and Tomasina Liriano, were both musicians, fostering an environment steeped in musical tradition from his earliest years. His father played the accordion and his mother sang, exposing Rigoberto to the sounds of traditional Dominican folk music, *perico ripiao* and *campesina*, which would heavily influence his later work. He received his initial musical education from his father, learning to play the accordion around the age of seven. 

Torres’s early professional career began in the late 1940s, playing at local parties and celebrations in Monte Cristi and surrounding areas. He quickly gained a reputation as a talented and energetic accordionist. In 1951, at the age of 23, Torres moved to Santo Domingo, the Dominican capital, seeking greater opportunities. This move proved to be a turning point in his career. He initially struggled to find consistent work, performing in small clubs and radio programs, but he persevered. 

A significant breakthrough came in 1953 when he joined the band of Luis Alberti, a popular singer and bandleader. This association provided Torres with a wider audience and allowed him to refine his skills. He stayed with Alberti for approximately two years, learning the nuances of professional performance and stage presence. However, Torres felt creatively constrained by Alberti’s established style and sought to develop his own distinctive sound.

In 1955, Torres formed his own band, “Los Primos,” initially consisting of himself on accordion, Jose Manuel Calcaño on bass, and Rafael Tejeda on tambora (a Dominican double-headed drum). This trio quickly became a sensation, injecting a new energy and sophistication into merengue.  Torres’s compositions began to move away from the purely rural themes of traditional *perico ripiao*, incorporating urban influences and social commentary. 

Throughout the 1960s and 70s, Torres and Los Primos released a string of hit records that revolutionized the merengue genre. Songs like “Carabina 30-30” (1968), a song inspired by a popular rifle, “Guarina” (1971), and "Con La Chepa" (1974) became national anthems, played at every celebration and dance. He innovated by adding saxophone and other brass instruments to the traditional merengue instrumentation, creating a fuller, more complex sound. His compositions often featured witty lyrics and clever arrangements that appealed to a broad audience.  He recorded over 30 albums throughout his career, selling an estimated 2 million records.

Torres’s impact extended beyond musical innovation. He was a vocal advocate for Dominican musicians and fought for better recognition and compensation for their work. He also played a key role in popularizing merengue internationally, performing in numerous countries including the United States, Venezuela, Panama, and Puerto Rico. In 1975, he was awarded the “Orden de Cristóbal Colón” (Order of Christopher Columbus), the highest honor bestowed by the Dominican government, in recognition of his contributions to Dominican culture. 

In the later decades of his life, Torres continued to perform and record, though at a less frenetic pace. He mentored younger musicians and remained a beloved figure in Dominican society.  He experienced health challenges in his final years, including complications from diabetes. Rigoberto Torres passed away on October 23, 2005, in Santo Domingo at the age of 77, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most important and influential figures in the history of Dominican music. His contributions fundamentally reshaped merengue, transforming it from a regional folk music into a national symbol and a globally recognized genre.

title: Erich Hartmann
text:
Erich Hartmann, often called the “Black Devil” by Soviet pilots, was the most successful fighter ace in the history of aerial warfare. He was born on April 14, 1922, in Weissach, Württemberg, Germany, to Paul and Elisabeth Hartmann. His father, a medical doctor, instilled in him a disciplined upbringing and an early interest in aviation, frequently taking young Erich to airshows. His mother, though initially hesitant, eventually supported his ambition to become a pilot. Hartmann’s early education was marked by a rebellious streak, and he was often in trouble at school. He joined the Deutsches Jungflieger (National Youth Flying League) in 1936, gaining initial flight experience in gliders.

With the increasing militarization of Germany, Hartmann applied to join the Luftwaffe in 1939 but was rejected due to his parents’ disapproval of the Nazi regime, specifically his father’s anti-Nazi sentiments. He was eventually accepted in October 1940 and began basic training at Reichsschule für Luftwaffenfachunteroffiziere in Wildau. He then progressed to flying school at A/B 12 in Salzwedel, followed by advanced training at Jagdfliegerschule 5 in Wien-Aspern, Austria, completing his training in August 1942. 

Hartmann was then assigned to Jagdgeschwader 52 (JG 52), based on the Eastern Front, specifically around Stalingrad. He flew the Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighter aircraft for the entirety of his combat career. His first combat sorties were in the fall of 1942, and he quickly gained experience in the brutal air battles over Russia. His first confirmed victory came on November 8, 1942, shooting down a Soviet Polikarpov I-153 biplane. 

By 1943, Hartmann’s skills were rapidly developing. He was known for his exceptional marksmanship and his ability to assess a combat situation quickly. He credited a key element of his success to firing only when he had a clear, killing shot, rather than engaging in prolonged dogfights, minimizing his own risk.  On March 10, 1943, he scored his 12th victory, earning the Iron Cross 1st Class. He reached 52 victories by the end of 1943, and was awarded the German Cross in Gold on January 1, 1944. 

1944 was Hartmann’s most prolific year. He became a Staffelkapitän (squadron leader) within JG 52, leading 1./JG 52.  On August 25, 1944, he achieved his 301st victory, earning the Knight’s Cross with Oak Leaves and Swords.  By the end of the year, his score had risen to 352 confirmed victories, a staggering number.  He was promoted to Hauptmann (Captain) in January 1945.  He continued flying combat missions until the very end of the war, narrowly escaping capture several times. His final sortie was on May 8, 1945, where he shot down a Yak-9 shortly before Germany’s unconditional surrender. 

Throughout the war, Hartmann flew over 1,400 combat missions and was officially credited with 352 aerial victories, all against Soviet aircraft. He was shot down 14 times, bailed out once, and was wounded in action. Remarkably, he survived the war without sustaining a single serious injury.

Following Germany’s surrender, Hartmann surrendered to American forces and was subsequently handed over to the Soviet Union as a prisoner of war. He spent over eight years in Soviet prisons, enduring harsh conditions and facing accusations of war crimes. He was eventually repatriated to West Germany on October 15, 1955, as part of a prisoner exchange. 

After returning home, Hartmann rejoined the Luftwaffe, now part of the Bundeswehr, and served as an instructor. He retired from the military in 1965 with the rank of Oberstleutnant (Lieutenant Colonel). In later life, he became a successful businessman and authored an autobiography, *My Life*, published in 1971. He was a somewhat controversial figure, especially in Germany, due to his wartime service and association with the Nazi regime. Erich Hartmann died on September 24, 1993, in Weinheim, Germany, at the age of 71.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar, born Omar Nur in Mogadishu, Somalia, on January 12, 1976, was a prominent figure in the Somali-Canadian community and a dedicated advocate for youth empowerment and gang prevention. His life was marked by a dramatic transformation, shifting from involvement in gang activity in his youth to becoming a respected community leader who worked tirelessly to steer young people away from similar paths.

Omar’s early life was heavily influenced by the tumultuous political climate of Somalia in the 1980s and early 1990s. The collapse of Siad Barre’s regime in 1991 plunged the country into civil war, leading to widespread violence and instability. At the age of 14, in 1990, Omar and his family fled Somalia, seeking refuge in Canada. They initially settled in Montreal, Quebec, before relocating to Toronto, Ontario, in 1993. The family’s experiences as refugees and newcomers to Canada shaped Omar’s understanding of marginalization and the challenges faced by immigrant communities.

Upon arriving in Toronto, Omar quickly became involved with the Dixon Bloods, a notorious street gang operating in the city’s west end, specifically in the Jamestown Crescent area. By the mid-1990s, he had risen through the ranks, becoming a significant figure within the gang. His involvement encompassed various criminal activities, and he spent a considerable portion of his youth navigating the complexities and dangers of gang life. However, a pivotal moment occurred in 1998 when he was shot five times during a gang-related altercation. This near-fatal experience served as a catalyst for change.

Following his recovery, Omar began to re-evaluate his life and the impact of his choices. He recognized the destructive cycle of violence and the lack of opportunities contributing to youth involvement in gangs.  In 2003, he founded the Youth Association for Advancement (YAA), a non-profit organization dedicated to providing at-risk youth with support, mentorship, and alternatives to gang life. YAA focused on educational programs, employment training, and recreational activities. 

Omar’s approach was unique in that he leveraged his lived experience and existing relationships within the community, including former gang members, to build trust and credibility. He wasn’t perceived as an outsider lecturing youth, but rather as someone who understood their struggles and could offer a realistic pathway out. YAA quickly gained recognition for its effectiveness in reducing youth violence and promoting positive social change in the Jamestown area.  Over the years, the organization expanded its reach, serving hundreds of young people and receiving funding from various sources, including the City of Toronto and private donors. 

In 2006, Omar received the Queen Elizabeth II Golden Jubilee Medal for his community service. He continued to be a vocal advocate for addressing the root causes of youth crime, emphasizing the need for investment in social programs, education, and employment opportunities. He frequently spoke at schools, community events, and government forums, sharing his personal story and advocating for systemic change.  He also worked closely with the Toronto Police Service, often acting as a liaison between law enforcement and the community, helping to facilitate communication and build trust.

Tragically, Nuh Omar’s life was cut short on November 19, 2014, when he was fatally shot in a targeted attack in the parking lot of a Scarborough restaurant. He was 38 years old. The circumstances surrounding his death remain a subject of ongoing investigation, though it is widely believed to be linked to his past involvement with gangs and his efforts to mediate conflicts within the community.  His death prompted an outpouring of grief and remembrance from across Toronto, with many acknowledging the profound impact he had made on the lives of countless young people.

title: A. K. Ramanujan
text:
Attipat Krishnaswami Ramanujan was born on June 16, 1929, in Mysore, Karnataka, India, to Attipat Krishnaswami and his wife, Ghantimathi. His father was a lawyer and amateur astronomer, and his mother a homemaker with a strong interest in Kannada poetry. Ramanujan was the youngest of three children, having an older brother and sister. His early education took place at Bishop Cotton Boys’ School in Bangalore, and later at The Hindu High School, Mysore. He demonstrated an early aptitude for languages, though initially showed more interest in botany and zoology. He began writing poetry in English during his teenage years, significantly influenced by the poetry of W. B. Yeats. 

Ramanujan completed his B.A. in English Literature from the University of Mysore in 1950, graduating with honors. He then pursued an M.A. in English and a diploma in Journalism, both also from the University of Mysore, finishing in 1951 and 1952 respectively. Following his studies, he worked briefly as a lecturer in English at the University of Mysore (1952-1953) and then as a government college teacher in Karnataka (1953-1958). This period saw the beginnings of his serious engagement with translation, particularly of classical Tamil poetry, initially as a personal exploration sparked by a chance encounter with a collection of poems.

A pivotal moment arrived in 1959 when Ramanujan received a fellowship from the Ford Foundation to study creative writing at the University of Iowa, in Iowa City, Iowa, USA. He arrived in the US with his wife, Kamala, and their two children. He completed his MFA in Creative Writing in 1962 and continued at Iowa, earning a Ph.D. in Linguistics in 1964 with a dissertation titled “The Structure of Meaning in Selected Tamil Poems.”  This marked a shift in his academic focus, blending his literary sensibilities with a rigorous linguistic approach.

Ramanujan began his academic career as an assistant professor of English at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in 1965. He remained there for nearly two decades, becoming a full professor in 1973.  During this time, he cemented his reputation as a major poet and translator. His first book of poems, *Poems* (1965), received the PEN/Oakland Josephine Miles Award.  His subsequent poetry collections, including *Relations* (1971), *The Striders* (1976), and *Second Sight* (1986), garnered widespread critical acclaim for their innovative use of language, their exploration of Indian-American identity, and their unique blend of personal and cultural experience.

However, Ramanujan’s most significant contribution arguably lies in his translations of classical Tamil poetry.  He published *The Interior Landscape* (1966), a groundbreaking collection of translations of Sangam poems (circa 300 BCE to 300 CE), introducing this ancient literary tradition to a Western audience.  He followed this with *Poems of Love and War from the Soongam* (1985), a more extensive and rigorously annotated selection.  These translations were not literal renderings but poetic re-creations, informed by his linguistic expertise and a deep understanding of the cultural context. 

In 1992, Ramanujan moved to the University of Chicago as a professor in the Committee on Southern Asian Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature.  He continued to publish and teach, focusing on Indian languages and literature, translation theory, and the relationship between language and culture. A controversial incident occurred in 1994 when the Indian government rejected several of his essays for inclusion in a collection to be published by the Sahitya Akademi (India’s National Academy of Letters), citing their perceived negative portrayal of Indian culture. This sparked a significant debate about academic freedom and censorship in India.

A. K. Ramanujan died on July 13, 1996, in Chicago, Illinois, at the age of 67, after a long battle with illness. His posthumous collections, *Collected Poems* (1997) and *The Black Helicopter* (2000), further solidified his legacy. He left behind a substantial body of work that continues to be studied and celebrated for its intellectual rigor, poetic beauty, and profound exploration of identity, belonging, and the complexities of translation.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on November 12, 1928, to parents of Spanish and Italian descent. His father, a civil engineer, instilled in him a precise, analytical approach, while his mother, an amateur botanist, fostered a deep love of plants and an understanding of their properties. This dual influence would prove pivotal in shaping his future career. He spent his childhood summers at his maternal grandfather’s estate in the pampas, a vast Argentinian grassland, where he observed and catalogued native flora, developing a keen eye for plant composition and the impact of landscape on atmosphere. 

Suarez initially followed his father’s profession, enrolling in the University of Buenos Aires’ School of Engineering in 1946. However, he found the rigid structure and focus on technical drawing unsatisfying. After two years, in 1948, he abandoned engineering to pursue studies in landscape architecture at the École Nationale Supérieure du Paysage Versailles in France. This marked a turning point, allowing him to combine his inherited analytical skills with his passion for botany. He graduated in 1952 with honors, having been particularly influenced by the work of Russian landscape architect Leonid Sabsovich, whose emphasis on naturalistic planting resonated with Suarez’s own aesthetic.

Upon graduation, Suarez spent several years travelling throughout Europe, working briefly with prominent landscape firms in Italy and Spain. In 1955, he established his own practice, ‘Diego Suarez Diseño de Jardines’, initially based in Paris. His early commissions were largely for private gardens belonging to affluent clients, often aristocrats and industrialists. He quickly gained a reputation for creating sophisticated, subtly dramatic spaces that prioritized a harmonious relationship between architecture and nature. 

A key commission in 1962, the gardens for the Villa Hügel, the former Krupp family estate in Essen, Germany, brought him international recognition. He transformed the formal, somewhat sterile gardens into a series of interconnected spaces inspired by the surrounding Bergisches Land landscape, introducing native plant species and a more relaxed, flowing design.  This project showcased his signature style: a blend of modern functionality, classical proportions, and a meticulous attention to plant selection. 

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, Suarez's practice expanded, undertaking large-scale public projects. He designed the gardens for the Musée Louis Vouland in Lausanne, Switzerland (completed 1978), creating a contemplative space that complemented the museum's collection of Asian art.  He also designed the extensive grounds of the Château de Courances in Essonne, France (1981-1986), restoring historic features while integrating contemporary landscaping techniques.  He completed over 150 projects across Europe, and notably, returned to Argentina in 1992 to redesign the formal gardens of the Casa Rosada, the presidential palace in Buenos Aires. This was a particularly challenging commission, requiring him to balance historical preservation with the needs of a modern government building.

Suarez's work was characterized by a restrained elegance, a sophisticated use of colour and texture, and a strong emphasis on creating gardens that felt both natural and purposefully designed. He avoided ostentation, preferring to let the plants themselves be the stars. He favoured a limited palette of plants, often utilizing variations within a single species to create subtle effects. He also pioneered the use of groundcover plants to reduce maintenance and create a more naturalistic look. 

He authored three books on garden design, ‘Jardins: L’Art de Vivre en Plein Air’ (1983), ‘The Contemporary Garden’ (1990), and ‘Espacios Verdes’ (1998) which were translated into multiple languages and became influential texts for aspiring landscape architects.  He received numerous awards throughout his career, including the Grand Prix du Paysage in France in 1987 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires in 2001.

Diego Suarez continued to work well into his eighties, accepting smaller, more private commissions. He died in Paris on July 18, 2015, at the age of 86, leaving behind a legacy of beautifully designed gardens that continue to inspire and delight visitors around the world. His designs remain renowned for their timeless quality and their ability to create spaces that are both aesthetically pleasing and deeply harmonious with the natural environment.

title: Vujadin Savić
text:
Vujadin Savić was born on January 27, 1930, in the village of Grabovac, near Gornji Milanovac, in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. His parents, Milosav and Milica, were farmers. He grew up in a modest household alongside his brother, Predrag, and sister, Radmila. Savić’s early life was marked by the hardships of rural existence and the looming shadow of World War II. He received his primary education in Grabovac and later attended the gymnasium (high school) in Gornji Milanovac, completing his studies in 1949.

Following his gymnasium graduation, Savić enrolled in the Faculty of Electrical Engineering at the University of Belgrade in 1949. He successfully completed his undergraduate studies in 1953 and continued his education, earning a Master of Science degree in 1956. He remained at the University, becoming a teaching assistant and beginning a research career focused on high-voltage engineering and electrical insulation.  He defended his doctoral dissertation in 1961, earning a PhD in Electrical Engineering, and was subsequently appointed as a docent (assistant professor) at the same faculty.

Savić’s career trajectory was rapid. He was promoted to associate professor in 1965 and full professor in 1970.  His research quickly gained international recognition, specializing in the breakdown voltage of insulating materials, particularly under pulsed high-voltage stress. He became a leading authority in the field, publishing over 200 scientific papers in prestigious international journals and presenting his work at numerous conferences across Europe, North America, and Asia.  A significant portion of his research revolved around the development of new insulating materials and techniques for high-voltage equipment, contributing directly to advancements in power transmission and distribution.

In 1973, Savić was elected as a full member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), a prestigious recognition of his scientific accomplishments. He served actively within SANU, holding various positions and contributing to numerous studies and initiatives. He became a corresponding member in 1969 before gaining full membership.  He championed the importance of scientific research for national development and advocated for increased investment in technological innovation within Yugoslavia. 

Beyond his academic and research work, Savić played a critical role in the development of Yugoslavia’s electrical energy sector. He consulted with major power companies and industrial enterprises, providing expertise on high-voltage systems and equipment. He was involved in the design and testing of transformers, circuit breakers, and other critical components of the national power grid. He was also a key figure in establishing national standards for high-voltage testing and safety.  He received the "October Award" – a significant Yugoslavian national award for science and technology – in 1977 for his contributions to the field.

Throughout his career, Savić mentored numerous students, many of whom went on to become prominent engineers and researchers themselves. He was known for his rigorous academic standards and his dedication to fostering a new generation of scientists. He held visiting professor positions at several international universities, including the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in the United States, further disseminating his knowledge and expertise globally.

Following his retirement from the University of Belgrade in 1993, Savić continued his research and remained an active member of SANU. He remained a highly sought-after consultant for industry and government agencies.  He was a recipient of numerous other accolades, including the Nikola Tesla Award in 1989, recognizing his lifetime achievements in electrical engineering.  Vujadin Savić passed away on December 12, 2015, in Belgrade, at the age of 85. His legacy continues through his extensive body of work and the impact he had on the advancement of electrical engineering in Yugoslavia and beyond.

title: Cobhams Asuquo
text:
Cobhams Asuquo was born on November 6, 1982, in Lagos, Nigeria, to a family with a strong musical background. His father, a lawyer, played the piano, and his mother was a professor of music. This early exposure profoundly influenced his development. However, Cobhams was born with glaucoma, a condition that led to total blindness at the age of three. Despite this significant challenge, his parents were committed to providing him with a normal upbringing and education, enrolling him in regular primary and secondary schools. He attended Kings College, Lagos, completing his secondary education in 1999. 

Cobhams began learning to play the piano at the age of six, initially through self-teaching and later with formal lessons. He demonstrated a natural aptitude for music, quickly progressing and developing his skills. He also learned to play other instruments, including the guitar and drums. While at Kings College, he formed a band with close friends, performing covers and original compositions. This period solidified his passion for creating music and performing. 

His professional music career began in 2005, initially as a backing vocalist and instrumentalist. He worked extensively with the renowned Nigerian singer, Asa, contributing significantly to her critically acclaimed debut album, *Asa* (2007). Cobhams played a pivotal role in writing and producing several tracks on the album, including the hit song “Fire on the Mountain.” This collaboration launched him into the Nigerian music industry spotlight. He was credited as a producer on the album, but his contributions were initially largely unacknowledged publicly.

Following the success of *Asa*, Cobhams established himself as a highly sought-after music producer and songwriter. He founded Cobhams Asuquo Productions (CAP), his own music production company. Over the next decade, he produced numerous hit songs for a diverse range of Nigerian artists, including Omawumi, Banky W, Davido, Tiwa Savage, Yemi Alade, and many others. He is credited with producing Omawumi’s debut album, *Wonder* (2008), which contained the hit single "Today's My Day."
