She appeared in television movies and guest starred on shows like “Diff'rent Strokes” and “The Love Boat.” She also returned to the stage, performing in numerous plays and musicals. In the 1980s, she took on the role of Golda Meir in a touring production of “Golda,” receiving positive reviews for her portrayal of the former Israeli Prime Minister. She continued performing "Golda" for several years, including a Broadway run in 1980-1981.

In 2009, Harper was diagnosed with terminal breast cancer, which had metastasized to her lungs. Despite the diagnosis and undergoing treatment, she continued to work, appearing on “Dancing with the Stars” in 2013, though she had to withdraw due to health complications. She publicly shared her battle with cancer, becoming an advocate for cancer awareness and research.  Her memoir, "I Rhoda," co-written with Stuart Shea, was published in 2013, detailing her life and career. 

Valerie Harper passed away on August 30, 2019, at the age of 80, at her home in Los Angeles, California. She was married to Richard Schacker from 1964 until his death in 2003. They had one daughter, Cristina Harper. Her legacy remains cemented as a groundbreaking comedic actress who brought joy and relatability to audiences for decades, particularly through her iconic portrayal of Rhoda Morgenstern.

title: Sérgio Moraes
text:
Sérgio Moraes was born Sérgio de Moraes Rego on December 27, 1941, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, into a family deeply connected to the world of music. His father, João de Moraes Rego, was a renowned classical music critic for the *Jornal do Brasil* newspaper, a position he held for over four decades, and his mother, Helena Fleischer, was a pianist. This upbringing immersed young Sérgio in a rich musical environment from the very beginning. He began formal piano studies at the age of six with the distinguished Brazilian pianist and pedagogue, Magdalena Tagliaferro, a former student of Arthur Rubinstein. Tagliaferro remained a crucial influence throughout his life, shaping his technical foundation and artistic sensibilities.

Moraes continued his musical education at the Escola de Música da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), graduating in 1963 with a degree in piano performance.  He furthered his studies abroad, receiving a scholarship to attend the École Normale de Musique de Paris from 1964 to 1966, where he studied with the celebrated French pianist Pierre Bernac, a prominent interpreter of Debussy and Fauré. Bernac’s influence steered Moraes towards French Impressionist music, a repertoire he would champion throughout his career. He also attended masterclasses with Nadia Boulanger, arguably the most influential composition teacher of the 20th century, solidifying his understanding of musical structure and interpretation.

Returning to Brazil in 1966, Moraes began a multifaceted career as a pianist, teacher, and musicologist. He quickly established himself as a highly respected solo performer, appearing with major Brazilian orchestras including the Orquestra Sinfônica Brasileira (OSB) and the Orquestra Sinfônica do Estado de São Paulo (OSESP). He performed extensively throughout Brazil, and also toured internationally, including appearances in Europe, North America, and Latin America. He was particularly known for his interpretations of Chopin, Debussy, and Brazilian composers like Heitor Villa-Lobos.

In 1972, Moraes earned a doctorate in Musicology from the Universidade de São Paulo (USP), with a dissertation focusing on the piano music of Camargo Guarnieri. This marked a turning point in his career, leading him to dedicate a significant portion of his time to scholarly research and writing. He became a leading authority on Brazilian music, publishing numerous articles and books, including a comprehensive study of Villa-Lobos's piano works, considered a standard reference. He also edited critical editions of works by Brazilian composers, preserving and promoting their legacy.

From 1976, Moraes became a professor at the Escola de Comunicações e Artes da Universidade de São Paulo (ECA-USP), where he taught piano, music history, and musicology for over thirty years, influencing generations of Brazilian musicians. He served as the head of the music department at ECA-USP for several terms. His pedagogical approach was known for its rigor and emphasis on understanding the historical and cultural context of music. 

Throughout his career, Moraes received numerous awards and accolades. He was a member of the Academia Brasileira de Música (Brazilian Academy of Music) and was honored with the Prêmio Carlos Gomes, a prestigious award recognizing outstanding contributions to Brazilian musical culture, in 1998. He was also a recipient of the Ordem do Mérito Cultural, awarded by the Brazilian government for distinguished service to the arts.

Sérgio Moraes continued to perform and teach well into his later years, maintaining a vibrant presence in the Brazilian musical landscape. He passed away on April 28, 2016, in São Paulo, at the age of 74, leaving behind a lasting legacy as a gifted pianist, a dedicated educator, and a prominent musicologist who played a crucial role in the preservation and promotion of Brazilian musical heritage. His recordings, scholarly writings, and the influence he had on his students continue to be celebrated and studied today.

title: Amr Shabana
text:
Amr Mohamed Shabana, widely regarded as one of the greatest squash players of all time, was born on September 19, 1978, in Alexandria, Egypt. His father, Mohamed Shabana, was a renowned squash player himself, reaching a career-high world ranking of number 5 in the 1970s, and played a pivotal role in fostering Amr’s early interest and development in the sport. Amr began playing squash at the age of six, initially learning the game at the Alexandria Sporting Club, a traditional hub for squash in Egypt. He was quickly identified as a prodigy, displaying exceptional talent and dedication. 

Shabana's early competitive career saw him dominate junior tournaments. He won the World Junior Squash Championships in 1996 in Peterborough, Canada, cementing his status as a rising star. This victory, at the age of 18, signaled his readiness for the professional ranks.  He turned professional in 1996, joining the Professional Squash Association (PSA) tour.

His initial years on the PSA Tour were marked by consistent improvement and gradual ascension. Shabana steadily climbed the rankings, showcasing a powerful and intelligent playing style characterized by deceptive shot-making, exceptional court coverage, and a relentless work ethic. He began making notable inroads into major tournaments, regularly reaching quarter-finals and semi-finals. 

The breakthrough season for Shabana was 2003. He won his first major PSA title at the Qatar International Squash Championships in Doha in November 2003, defeating David Palmer in the final. This victory propelled him into the top 10 of the world rankings.  He carried this momentum into 2004, culminating in his first World Open title, held in Cairo, Egypt, in December of that year. This was a particularly significant victory playing on home soil, defeating fellow Egyptian and long-time rival, Ahmed Barada, in the final.

Shabana’s reign as World Number 1 began in June 2006, displacing Thierry Lincan. He held the top ranking for a total of 36 months, a testament to his consistency and dominance. During this period, he secured a further three World Open titles – in 2007 in Eindhoven, Netherlands, in 2008 in Luxor, Egypt, and in 2009 in Kuwait.  He became the first player to win the World Open three times consecutively.

Throughout his career, Shabana accumulated an impressive record of 38 PSA Tour titles. He was renowned for his competitive spirit and tactical acumen, often outmaneuvering opponents with his strategic play.  He faced stiff competition from players such as David Palmer, James Willstrop, Nick Matthew, and Ramy Ashour, consistently proving himself against the best. His rivalry with Ashour, in particular, became a defining feature of the sport in the late 2000s and early 2010s, with both players engaging in numerous thrilling encounters.

Shabana's last tournament win was the 2012 Kuwait International Squash Championships.  Injuries, particularly to his Achilles tendon and knee, began to take their toll in the later stages of his career, impacting his movement and ultimately contributing to his retirement in 2014 at the age of 35. He announced his retirement following a second-round loss at the 2014 Allam British Open. 

Following his retirement from professional play, Shabana remained involved in squash. He transitioned into a coaching role, working with promising young players and sharing his extensive knowledge of the game. He also served as a consultant and ambassador for squash development programs in Egypt. He has been involved in mentoring current Egyptian players, including the current world number one, Ali Farag.  Shabana is married and has two children. He continues to live in Cairo and is considered a national hero in Egypt, having significantly raised the profile of the sport within the country.

title: Charmion King
text:
Charmion King was born on July 26, 1908, in Dayton, Ohio, to William and Florence King. Her full name was Charmion Drexel King, and she came from a family with a strong artistic inclination; her mother was a painter and her father a journalist. From a very young age, Charmion demonstrated an aptitude for swimming, encouraged by her parents who believed in physical fitness. She began formal swimming lessons at the Dayton YMCA at age six, quickly excelling under the tutelage of coach David Armbruster. 

By 1920, at the age of twelve, King had already begun to attract attention for her swimming prowess. She competed in the inaugural Women’s National Amateur Athletic Association (WNAAA) national championships in Hawaii, winning the 100-yard freestyle and setting a new American record of 1 minute, 13.2 seconds. This victory marked the beginning of a distinguished competitive career. She continued to break records throughout the 1920s, specializing in freestyle and backstroke. 

In 1922, King set a world record in the 100-yard freestyle, clocking in at 1:08.8, a time that stood for over four years. She was a dominant force in women’s swimming, winning 39 national championships and setting numerous American and world records.  Her successes included multiple victories in the 100-yard and 150-yard freestyle, as well as the 100-yard backstroke.  She was particularly known for her efficient and powerful crawl stroke. 

The 1924 Summer Olympics in Paris presented King with her most significant opportunity. Swimming was a relatively new sport for women at the Olympic level, and the American team was considered a strong contender.  King competed in the 100-meter freestyle, 400-meter freestyle, and the 4x100-meter freestyle relay. She won a gold medal in the 100-meter freestyle, finishing in 1 minute, 12.4 seconds, and a bronze medal in the 4x100-meter freestyle relay alongside teammates Gertrude Ederle, Elizabeth Duke, and Marion Lohman.  Despite her individual success, the American team was overshadowed by the phenomenal performance of Ederle, who later that year would become the first woman to swim the English Channel.

Beyond competition, King was a pioneer in promoting women’s swimming. She actively participated in exhibitions and demonstrations aimed at encouraging wider participation in the sport.  She penned articles for popular magazines promoting physical fitness and the benefits of swimming, and actively sought sponsorship to support her travels and training.  She was frequently featured in newspaper articles, celebrated as a role model for young women.

King retired from competitive swimming in 1928, at the age of 20, after participating in the Olympic trials, though she did not qualify for the Amsterdam Games. She pursued a career in physical education, earning a Bachelor of Science degree from the University of Chicago in 1932. Following graduation, she worked as a physical education instructor at the Edgewood School for Girls in Greenwich, Connecticut, for over three decades, retiring in 1970. 

During her time at Edgewood, she implemented innovative physical education programs and continued to advocate for women’s athletics. She also remained involved in the swimming community, serving as a judge and official at various swimming competitions. In 1968, she was inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame, recognizing her lifetime contributions to the sport. 

Charmion King lived a relatively private life after her retirement from teaching. She remained unmarried and maintained a residence in Greenwich, Connecticut. She passed away on February 23, 1993, at the age of 84, in Greenwich. Her legacy extends beyond her Olympic medals and record-breaking swims; she was a champion for women’s sports and a dedicated educator who inspired generations of young women to embrace physical activity and strive for excellence.

title: Maddy Crippen
text:
Madeline “Maddy” Crippen, born on January 26, 1938, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, was a pioneering American television news director, known for breaking barriers for women in broadcast journalism and for her innovative approach to local news programming. She was the daughter of Walter and Dorothy Crippen, and grew up in a household that encouraged intellectual curiosity and civic engagement. She attended the University of Wisconsin–Madison, graduating with a degree in journalism in 1960. While at UW-Madison, she was involved in student broadcasting, honing her skills at WHA-TV, the university’s educational television station. 

Crippen began her professional career in 1960 as a production assistant at WMTV in Madison, Wisconsin, quickly moving up to become a reporter and producer. She transitioned to Milwaukee in 1965, joining WTMJ-TV (Channel 4), then a CBS affiliate. Initially working as a reporter covering a wide range of beats, including social issues and local politics, she quickly demonstrated a talent for storytelling and an ability to connect with audiences. By 1968, she was named a news producer, a relatively uncommon position for a woman at the time.

Her breakthrough came in 1971 when she was appointed news director at WTMJ-TV, becoming one of the first women in the United States to lead a major market television newsroom. This appointment was particularly significant as Milwaukee was the 15th largest television market in the country at the time. Crippen immediately began to reshape the station’s news coverage. Recognizing a gap in programming that addressed the concerns of everyday citizens, she spearheaded the creation of “Milwaukee Magazine,” a weekly magazine-style show that debuted in September 1972. 

“Milwaukee Magazine” was a radical departure from the traditional, hard-news format prevalent at the time. It focused on human-interest stories, local arts and culture, consumer advocacy, and in-depth investigations into issues affecting the Milwaukee community. The program quickly gained popularity, consistently achieving high ratings and winning numerous awards, including a regional Emmy Award in 1975 for its coverage of the city’s housing crisis. It was a model for similar magazine-style news programs that emerged across the country in the following years. 

Crippen’s leadership extended beyond “Milwaukee Magazine.” She fostered a collaborative newsroom environment and encouraged investigative reporting. Under her direction, WTMJ-TV became known for its comprehensive coverage of local government, its proactive consumer reporting, and its commitment to showcasing the diversity of the Milwaukee area. She actively recruited and mentored young journalists, including many women and minorities, helping to diversify the ranks of broadcast news. In 1978, she oversaw the launch of a 10 pm newscast, expanding the station’s news offerings and further solidifying its position as a leading news provider.

In 1982, Crippen left WTMJ-TV and moved into public service, accepting a position as Director of Communications for the Milwaukee Public Museum. She remained in that role for nearly a decade, overseeing the museum’s public relations, marketing, and educational outreach efforts. She was instrumental in securing funding for new exhibits and programs and in raising the museum’s profile within the community. 

Following her tenure at the museum, Crippen became a consultant, offering her expertise in communications and media relations to various organizations. She also remained active in journalism education, lecturing at universities and mentoring aspiring journalists. She was a member of the Wisconsin Broadcasters Association Hall of Fame, inducted in 1998, recognizing her significant contributions to the state’s broadcasting industry. 

Maddy Crippen died on July 28, 2016, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, at the age of 78, after a battle with cancer. She never married and had no children. Her legacy endures as a testament to her innovative vision, her dedication to public service, and her pioneering role in opening doors for women in the field of broadcast journalism. Her commitment to impactful, community-focused news continues to influence local news programming today.

title: Julie Bishop
text:
Julie Bishop was born Julie Maxine Bishop on July 17, 1966, in Lobethal, South Australia, a small Adelaide Hills town with strong German heritage. Her parents, Doug and Margaret Bishop, were both involved in local politics; her father was a local councillor and her mother a schoolteacher. Bishop attended Lobethal Lutheran School and then Urrbrae Agricultural High School, excelling in debating and public speaking. She demonstrated early ambition and leadership qualities, becoming school captain in 1983. 

Bishop commenced a Bachelor of Arts degree at the University of Adelaide in 1984, majoring in Government and Public Policy. She deferred her studies in 1985 to work as a research assistant to Liberal Member for Mayo, Dudley Hausler. This experience sparked her interest in a political career and allowed her to gain practical insights into parliamentary processes. She completed her degree in 1988, graduating with Honours. Following university, Bishop worked as an associate to Justice Jane Matthews of the South Australian Equal Opportunity Tribunal, furthering her legal understanding.

She then pursued a legal career, qualifying as a solicitor in 1990 after completing the Law Society of South Australia’s Articles of Clerkship. Bishop worked at legal firms Minter Ellison and later Clayton Utz, specializing in commercial litigation. She became a partner at Clayton Utz in 1998, a significant accomplishment at the age of 32. During her time in legal practice, she handled a diverse range of cases, including complex commercial disputes and advising on corporate governance.

Bishop’s entry into federal politics came in 1998 when she successfully contested the Division of Curtin in Western Australia for the Liberal Party. She defeated longstanding Labor incumbent, Allan Griffiths, winning with a 5.8% swing. She was immediately appointed to the parliamentary secretary role assisting the Minister for Defence, John Moore. In 2003, she was promoted to Minister for Children and Youth, then, in 2005, Minister for Education and Youth. 

A key period in her career began in 2007 when she was appointed Shadow Minister for Treasury, a role she held until 2013. During this time, she was a vocal critic of the Labor government’s economic policies. Following the Liberal/National Coalition’s victory in the 2013 federal election, Bishop was appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs in Tony Abbott’s cabinet. 

As Foreign Minister, Bishop significantly raised Australia’s international profile. She focused on strengthening ties with countries in the Indo-Pacific region and played a key role in negotiating the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement. She oversaw the response to the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 in 2014, leading Australia’s efforts to secure justice for the victims. She also championed women’s leadership in foreign policy and advocated for human rights on the international stage. Bishop was the first woman to hold the position of Foreign Minister in Australia.

She retained the Foreign Affairs portfolio under Malcolm Turnbull, becoming the Deputy Leader of the Liberal Party in 2017 following the leadership change. This made her a key figure in the government. However, the Liberal Party lost the 2019 federal election, and Bishop subsequently resigned from her positions, including the deputy leadership. 

Since leaving parliament, Bishop has pursued a successful career in the private sector. In 2020, she joined the board of Palladium, an international development consultancy. She also serves on the boards of several other companies. Bishop has been a frequent commentator on political and international affairs, and in 2021, she published her memoir, "Halftime", which became a bestseller. In January 2024, she was appointed as the Chancellor of Murdoch University. She continues to be a prominent public figure, offering perspectives on current events and advocating for issues she is passionate about. Bishop remains unmarried and resides in Perth, Western Australia.

title: Aleksandar Kolarov
text:
Aleksandar Kolarov was born on November 10, 1985, in Belgrade, Serbia, then part of Yugoslavia. His early footballing education began at Red Star Belgrade’s youth academy in 1995, where he spent the next eight years developing his skills. Initially a central midfielder, coaches recognised his powerful left foot and versatility, gradually shifting him to the left-back position. He made his senior debut for Red Star on March 26, 2004, in a Yugoslav League match against FK Sutjeska Nikšić. He quickly established himself as a regular, playing 38 matches and scoring four goals across all competitions for the club. 

His performances attracted attention from abroad, and in the summer of 2006, Kolarov moved to OFK Belgrade for a reported fee of €600,000. He spent one season with OFK, featuring in 28 league games and scoring twice. This period further honed his attacking prowess from full-back, contributing with assists and powerful shots. His consistent displays caught the eye of Lazio sporting director Igli Tare, leading to a transfer to the Italian club in July 2007 for approximately €3.5 million.

Kolarov’s time at Lazio, under coach Delio Rossi, proved pivotal. He immediately became a key player, showcasing his dynamism, crossing ability and set-piece expertise. He played 171 games for the *Biancocelesti* across all competitions, scoring 25 goals. A standout moment came on November 22, 2009, when he scored a stunning free-kick against Livorno, demonstrating the power and accuracy that would become a trademark of his game. He also helped Lazio win the Coppa Italia in 2009, defeating Sampdoria 6-5 on penalties after a 1-1 draw, playing the full 120 minutes of the final.

His consistently impressive form led to a move to Manchester City in July 2010, under manager Roberto Mancini, for a reported fee of around £16 million. He became a crucial component of City's evolving squad, providing width and attacking threat. During his seven seasons at the Etihad Stadium, Kolarov amassed 247 appearances, scoring 22 goals. He was a key figure in City’s Premier League title wins in 2012 and 2014, as well as their FA Cup triumph in 2011 and League Cup victories in 2014, 2016 and 2018. He captained Manchester City on several occasions, demonstrating his leadership qualities.

In July 2017, at the age of 31, Kolarov made a surprising move to Roma, joining the Italian side for a fee of around €5 million. He reunited with former Manchester City manager Eusebio Di Francesco. He quickly adapted to his new surroundings, becoming a mainstay in the Roma defence and contributing significantly in attack.  He played 95 games for Roma, scoring nine goals. He experienced a Champions League semi-final run with Roma in the 2017-18 season, where they were narrowly defeated by Liverpool. 

Kolarov also enjoyed a long and successful international career with Serbia. He earned his first cap on November 15, 2008, in a friendly against Poland. He represented Serbia at the 2010 FIFA World Cup, the 2014 FIFA World Cup, and the 2018 FIFA World Cup. He captained the national team for a significant period, accumulating 94 caps and scoring 11 goals, making him one of the most capped players in Serbian history. He retired from international football in March 2021.

Following his departure from Roma in August 2020, Kolarov returned to Serbia to play for his boyhood club, Red Star Belgrade, on a one-year contract. He retired from professional football in June 2022, bringing an end to a distinguished 17-year career.  After retirement, Kolarov transitioned into a coaching role, taking on a position as an assistant coach with the Serbia national team in August 2023, working under Dragan Stojković.

title: Winston Churchill
text:
Winston Leonard Spencer-Churchill was born on November 30, 1874, at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, England, the son of Lord Randolph Churchill, a Conservative politician, and Jennie Jerome, an American socialite. His early childhood was largely marked by emotional distance from his parents; he was primarily raised by his nanny, Elizabeth Everest. He attended Harrow School in 1888, achieving moderate academic success but demonstrating a particular aptitude for history and English. He initially pursued a military career, entering the Royal Military College, Sandhurst in 1893. 

Commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars in 1895, Churchill sought active service and quickly found it, reporting as a war correspondent for the *Pioneer* and *Morning Post* newspapers during the Second Anglo-Boer War in South Africa beginning in 1899. He gained public attention for his daring escape from a Boer prisoner-of-war camp in December 1899, a feat that fueled his burgeoning reputation for courage and initiative. Upon his return to Britain, he resigned his commission and entered politics, being elected as the Conservative Member of Parliament for Oldham in 1900. 

Churchill's early parliamentary career saw him frequently crossing the political floor. He defected to the Liberal Party in 1904, disagreeing with Conservative policies on trade tariffs. He served as President of the Board of Trade from 1908 to 1910 under Prime Minister H.H. Asquith, introducing social reforms like labour exchanges and minimum wages. He then became Home Secretary in 1910, a position he held until 1911, during which he dealt with industrial unrest and suffragette protests. From 1911 to 1915, he served as First Lord of the Admiralty, modernizing the Royal Navy and preparing it for war. 

The disastrous Gallipoli Campaign in 1915, which he heavily advocated for, led to his demotion and temporary removal from the Admiralty. He served with the Royal Scots Fusiliers on the Western Front in France from 1916, before returning to government as Minister of Munitions in 1917 under David Lloyd George.  He played a significant role in coordinating war production. After the war, he served as Secretary of State for War and Air from 1919 to 1921, advocating for intervention against the Bolsheviks in Russia.

The 1920s and 1930s were a politically challenging period for Churchill.  He rejoined the Conservative Party in 1924 and served as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Stanley Baldwin from 1924 to 1929, controversially returning Britain to the gold standard in 1925. He lost his seat in the 1929 general election but was re-elected in 1931.  Throughout the 1930s, he became a vocal and largely isolated critic of the policy of appeasement towards Nazi Germany, warning of the growing threat posed by Adolf Hitler. He accurately predicted the increasing aggression of Germany in numerous speeches and writings.

Upon the outbreak of World War II in September 1939, Churchill was reappointed to the Admiralty.  Following Neville Chamberlain’s resignation in May 1940, Churchill became Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, forming a national government. His powerful oratory, particularly his speeches like “We shall fight on the beaches” (June 4, 1940) and “Their Finest Hour” (June 18, 1940), rallied the British public during the darkest days of the war. He forged a crucial alliance with the United States, working closely with President Franklin D. Roosevelt and later Harry S. Truman. He participated in key wartime conferences, including the Atlantic Conference (1941), the Casablanca Conference (1943), and the Yalta Conference (1945).

Despite leading Britain to victory in 1945, Churchill’s Conservative Party lost the general election in July of that year to Clement Attlee’s Labour Party. He served as Leader of the Opposition from 1945 to 1951. He was re-elected as Prime Minister in 1951, serving until 1955, focusing on foreign policy and maintaining Britain's international standing.  In 1953, he suffered a stroke, which impacted his health for the remainder of his life. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 "for his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for his brilliant oratory."  

Winston Churchill died on January 24, 1965, at his home in Chartwell, Kent, at the age of 90, following complications from his stroke. He was given a state funeral, attended by dignitaries from around the world, marking his lasting legacy as one of the 20th century’s most significant leaders.

title: Ezechiel N'Douassel
text:
Ezechiel N’Douassel, born on January 26, 1976, in Libreville, Gabon, was a professional footballer who carved a unique and remarkably consistent career primarily in the lower tiers of French football. While he never reached the heights of international stardom enjoyed by some of his countrymen, N’Douassel became a legendary figure for his prolific goalscoring record and unwavering dedication to the game, earning him the nickname “Le Roi” (The King) amongst fans.

N’Douassel’s early footballing education took place in Gabon, but details regarding his initial clubs remain scarce. He arrived in France as a teenager in the mid-1990s, initially joining the youth academy of AS Beauvais-Oise in 1994. He made his senior debut for Beauvais in the Championnat National, the third tier of French football, in the 1995-1996 season, appearing in 24 matches and scoring 8 goals. His performance attracted attention, and he moved to Amiens SC in 1996, again in the Championnat National. 

He spent two seasons with Amiens, becoming a key player and netting 23 goals in 63 appearances. This form led to a brief stint in Ligue 2 with Le Havre AC in 1998, but he found limited playing time and only featured in 12 games, scoring twice. He returned to the Championnat National in 1999, joining Étampes US. His time there was short-lived, and he soon moved to FC Rouen in the same league.

It was at Rouen, between 1999 and 2003, that N’Douassel truly began to establish himself as a consistent goalscorer. He scored an impressive 85 goals in 146 appearances, becoming the club’s all-time leading scorer, a record he still holds. This period cemented his reputation and attracted attention from clubs aiming for promotion. In 2003, he moved to US Créteil-Lusitanos, a team in Ligue 2. 

He spent three seasons with Créteil, scoring 34 goals in 86 appearances. While the team didn't achieve promotion to Ligue 1, N’Douassel consistently proved his worth as a reliable striker. In 2006, at the age of 30, he joined Amiens SC for a second spell, this time in Ligue 2.  He enjoyed a successful return, scoring 16 goals in 34 games during the 2006-2007 season.

However, his most celebrated period came with Clermont Foot, joining the club in 2007. Over six seasons, from 2007 to 2013, N’Douassel flourished, becoming a club icon. He played 214 games for Clermont, scoring a remarkable 95 goals, making him their all-time top scorer, surpassing his previous record at Rouen.  He was instrumental in Clermont’s consistent pushing for promotion to Ligue 1, although they ultimately fell short during his tenure. He achieved his highest league finish with Clermont in the 2010-2011 season, finishing 6th in Ligue 2.

N’Douassel also had a brief international career with the Gabon national team, earning 23 caps and scoring 5 goals between 2002 and 2011. He participated in the 2010 Africa Cup of Nations, held in Angola, where Gabon reached the quarter-finals.

After leaving Clermont Foot in 2013, N’Douassel continued to play professionally, moving to Amiens SC for a third spell in the Championnat National, then briefly to AS Vitré in 2014. He finally announced his retirement from professional football in 2015 at the age of 39, having played for over two decades. 

Following his retirement, N’Douassel remained connected to the sport. He completed his coaching badges and has since worked as a youth coach in the Auvergne region of France, specifically focusing on developing young talent. He is highly regarded within footballing circles in the region and is remembered fondly by fans of the clubs he played for, particularly Amiens and Clermont Foot, for his dedication, longevity, and impressive goalscoring record. He remains a respected and beloved figure in French lower league football.

title: Sheldon T. Mills
text:
Sheldon Theodore Mills, a prominent figure in American finance and a trailblazer for African Americans in the investment banking world, was born on November 29, 1956, in New York City. He was raised in the St. Albans neighborhood of Queens, a middle-class Black community that fostered a strong sense of achievement. His father, Theodore Mills, was a postal worker, and his mother, Vivian Mills, was a school teacher. This background instilled in him a strong work ethic and the importance of education. Mills attended Archbishop Molan High School in Queens, graduating in 1974. He then pursued higher education at Stanford University, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics in 1978. He continued his studies at Harvard Business School, graduating with a Master of Business Administration degree in 1981.

Mills’s career began on Wall Street at Goldman Sachs in 1981, joining as an associate in the Corporate Finance department. This was a significant achievement, as African Americans were vastly underrepresented in the high-finance world at the time. He quickly distinguished himself through his analytical skills and dedication, steadily climbing the ranks. He became a Vice President in 1987, and a Partner in 1990, making him one of the first African American partners in the firm’s history. During his 21-year tenure at Goldman Sachs, he specialized in mergers and acquisitions, advising companies on deals totaling billions of dollars. He was instrumental in several high-profile transactions, including the $10.3 billion merger of Bell Atlantic and NYNEX in 1997, and the $5.3 billion acquisition of Quaker Oats by PepsiCo in 2001. 

Beyond his deal-making prowess, Mills was a committed advocate for diversity within the firm and the broader financial industry. He actively mentored young professionals from underrepresented backgrounds and championed initiatives to increase recruitment and retention of minority employees. He served as the head of Goldman Sachs’ Pine Street leadership program, designed to cultivate future leaders within the company. 

In 2002, Mills left Goldman Sachs to join Wasserstein Perella & Co., a boutique investment bank, as a Managing Director. He was brought in specifically to build and lead the firm’s financial sponsors group, focusing on private equity clients. He successfully expanded the group’s business, forging strong relationships with prominent private equity firms.  

In 2006, Mills transitioned to a new phase of his career, becoming a Senior Advisor to Apollo Global Management, a leading alternative investment firm. He provided strategic advice on investments and played a key role in the firm’s expansion. Simultaneously, he became a member of the Board of Directors for several public companies, including Hess Corporation, where he served on the Audit Committee, and Viacom, now Paramount Global. He also served on the Board of Trustees for his alma mater, Stanford University, from 2008 to 2016, contributing to the university's financial oversight and strategic direction.

Throughout his career, Mills was recognized for his leadership and contributions to the financial community. He was consistently listed among the “100 Most Influential Black Executives in America” by *Savoy Magazine*. He was also a frequent speaker at industry events, sharing his insights on finance, diversity, and leadership. 

Sheldon T. Mills passed away on March 17, 2023, in New York City, at the age of 66, following a battle with cancer. His death was widely mourned throughout the financial world. He is remembered not only for his impressive career achievements but also for his commitment to mentoring and paving the way for future generations of diverse leaders in finance. He left behind his wife, Dr. Deborah C. Mills, and two daughters, Stephanie and Alexandra. His legacy continues to inspire those seeking to break barriers and create a more inclusive financial landscape.

title: Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay
text:
Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay, a pivotal figure in the development of Indian statistical methodology and a dedicated educator, was born on December 22, 1908, in the village of Talitpur, in the Nadia district of West Bengal, India. His father, Radhakrishna Mukhopadhyay, was a schoolteacher and his mother, Charubala Devi, instilled in him a strong emphasis on education and cultural values. He received his early education at the Talitpur High English School, consistently demonstrating exceptional aptitude in mathematics. He continued his studies at Presidency College, Calcutta, graduating with a Bachelor of Science in Physics in 1930, securing first class honours. 

While initially focused on physics, Mukhopadhyay’s academic path dramatically shifted after being introduced to the nascent field of statistics by Professor P.C. Mahalanobis at Presidency College. He joined the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI), founded by Mahalanobis in 1932, becoming one of its earliest recruits and a foundational pillar of its growth. He initially worked as a research assistant, quickly proving his talent for statistical analysis and contributing to early ISI projects focused on agricultural statistics and the analysis of monsoon rainfall patterns.

In 1938, Mukhopadhyay travelled to the London School of Economics, studying under the renowned statistician Karl Pearson, and earned a Sc.D. degree in Statistics in 1941. His doctoral dissertation, focused on sequential analysis, showcased his innovative thinking and laid the groundwork for much of his future research. He returned to India in 1942, amidst the complexities of World War II, and resumed his work at ISI, now facing challenges of wartime resource constraints and the need to contribute to national planning.

Mukhopadhyay’s contributions to statistical theory and application are substantial. He is particularly renowned for his work on sequential analysis, specifically the development of Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) designs and their application to industrial quality control and clinical trials. He published extensively on this topic, with key papers appearing in journals like *Biometrika* and *The Annals of Mathematical Statistics* throughout the 1940s and 50s.  He also made significant contributions to the theory of estimation, hypothesis testing, and design of experiments. Beyond purely theoretical work, he spearheaded the application of statistical methods to diverse fields including demography, economics, and public health. 

He held various key positions at ISI throughout his career. He became a Professor in 1946 and served as the Director of the Statistics Department. From 1954 to 1956, he was the Deputy Director of ISI, assisting Mahalanobis in the Institute’s administrative and research activities. He played a critical role in establishing ISI’s postgraduate programs and shaping the curriculum, fostering a generation of Indian statisticians.  He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society in 1952 and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association in 1956, recognizing his international stature in the field. 

Mukhopadhyay was also deeply involved in national planning and policy-making. He served on numerous government committees, advising on statistical aspects of the Five-Year Plans and contributing to the development of national sample surveys. His expertise was instrumental in establishing robust statistical infrastructure for India’s economic development. He was a member of the Planning Commission's Statistical Sub-Committee for a considerable period, contributing significantly to the statistical framework used for national planning. 

In his later life, Mukhopadhyay continued his research and teaching at ISI, focusing increasingly on the philosophical foundations of statistics and the ethical considerations in its application. He retired from ISI in 1972, but remained actively engaged in scholarly pursuits until his health declined. He received the Padma Bhushan, one of India’s highest civilian awards, in 1973, acknowledging his lifetime contributions to the field of statistics and to national development. Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay passed away on November 23, 1981, in Calcutta, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering statistician, a dedicated teacher, and a key architect of India's statistical capabilities.

title: Yordanka Donkova
text:
Yordanka Donkova was born on September 18, 1961, in Pavlikeni, Bulgaria, a small town known for its agricultural production. Her parents, Doncho and Penka Donkovi, were both involved in athletics, with her father being a long-distance runner and her mother a high jumper. This familial background instilled in her a love for sports from a young age. She initially showed promise in gymnastics, but at the age of 10, a coach identified her potential for hurdles, specifically the 100-meter hurdles. This early switch proved pivotal, setting the stage for a remarkable career.

Donkova began training at the Vasil Levski National Sports Academy in Sofia, Bulgaria, a national center for athletic development. Her coach, Ivan Ivanov, played a crucial role in shaping her technique and building her stamina. She quickly progressed through the ranks, demonstrating exceptional speed, agility, and a natural talent for clearing hurdles efficiently. Her international debut came in 1979, competing at the European Junior Championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland, where she finished sixth in the 100m hurdles. 

The early 1980s saw Donkova steadily improve, gaining valuable experience at major international events. She participated in the 1980 Summer Olympics in Moscow, reaching the semi-finals of the 100m hurdles. However, it was 1983 that marked her breakthrough. At the inaugural World Championships in Athletics held in Helsinki, Finland, on August 7, 1983, Donkova won the gold medal in the 100m hurdles, clocking a time of 12.38 seconds. This victory established her as a world-class athlete and a rising star in the sport.

The following year, the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles presented a significant opportunity. On August 5, 1984, Donkova competed in a thrilling 100m hurdles final, finishing in second place with a time of 12.35 seconds, behind American Glynis Nunn-Cearns who won in 12.34 seconds. This silver medal was a defining moment in Bulgarian Olympic history. 

Donkova reached the peak of her career in 1987. On August 29, 1987, in Varna, Bulgaria, she set a world record in the 100m hurdles, clocking an astonishing 12.21 seconds. This record stood for eight years, a testament to her incredible athleticism and training. She further cemented her dominance at the 1987 World Championships in Rome, Italy, winning her second gold medal in the 100m hurdles with a time of 12.38 seconds. 

She continued to compete at a high level throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s, participating in the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona, Spain, where she reached the semi-finals. While she didn’t add to her Olympic medal count, she remained a consistent performer on the international circuit. Donkova competed in a total of three Olympic Games (1980, 1984, 1992) and three World Championships (1983, 1987, 1991).

Yordanka Donkova formally retired from competitive athletics in 1993. Following her athletic career, she transitioned into coaching, dedicating herself to nurturing the next generation of Bulgarian hurdlers. She served as a coach at the Vasil Levski National Sports Academy, sharing her expertise and experience with aspiring athletes. She also became involved in sports administration, holding positions within the Bulgarian Athletics Federation. 

Throughout her life, Donkova has been recognized for her contributions to sport. She was named Bulgarian Sportswoman of the Year on multiple occasions, including 1983, 1985, 1986, and 1987. In 1999, she was inducted into the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) Hall of Fame.  Donkova remains a highly respected figure in Bulgarian athletics, remembered not only for her athletic achievements but also for her dedication to the sport and her role in inspiring generations of athletes. She currently resides in Sofia, Bulgaria, and continues to be a prominent voice in the Bulgarian sporting community.

title: Félix María Zuloaga
text:
Félix María Zuloaga y Ariza was born on January 26, 1846, in Madrid, Spain, into a family deeply entrenched in Spanish political and artistic circles. His father, Ignacio Zuloaga, was a respected painter and director of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, a position Félix would later hold. His mother, Julia Ariza, came from a family with strong liberal convictions. This familial blend of artistic talent and political awareness significantly shaped Félix’s early life. He initially pursued a legal career, enrolling in the Faculty of Law at the University of Madrid in 1862, earning his doctorate in 1865. However, his interests lay more with politics than jurisprudence. 

Zuloaga’s political career began relatively early, in 1871, when he was elected as a deputy for the province of Cuenca in the Cortes Generales, the Spanish parliament. He aligned himself with the Moderate Conservative party, a faction advocating for a constitutional monarchy but favoring order and centralisation over radical reforms. He would remain a deputy for various constituencies – Guadalajara, Madrid, and finally, Vizcaya – for much of the next three decades, becoming a prominent voice within the conservative political landscape. 

The turbulent political climate of Spain in the late 19th century, marked by frequent coups and constitutional changes, propelled Zuloaga into a position of significant power. Following a military uprising led by Brigadier General Arsenio Martínez Campos in December 1874, which effectively overthrew the First Spanish Republic, Zuloaga was instrumental in restoring the Bourbon monarchy. He played a key role in negotiating with Alfonso, then in exile, to accept the crown under certain conditions, drafting the “Manifesto of Sandhurst” which outlined those terms. 

This contribution led to his appointment as Prime Minister of Spain on January 5, 1875, a position he held for a relatively brief but impactful period of just under a year. His government focused on establishing stability, restoring traditional values, and consolidating royal authority. He oversaw the drafting of the Constitution of 1876, which remains a foundational document in Spanish constitutional history. This constitution, formally proclaimed on December 29, 1876, established a parliamentary monarchy, guaranteeing certain civil rights and outlining the powers of the crown and the Cortes.  

Despite his success in restoring the monarchy and crafting a new constitution, Zuloaga’s time as Prime Minister was marked by difficulties. He faced opposition from both radical republicans and more progressive conservatives who felt the new constitution did not go far enough in granting political freedoms. He was eventually forced to resign on March 12, 1876, due to pressure from within the Conservative party, specifically from Emilio Castelar, a former Republican who had briefly served as Prime Minister in the preceding Republic.

Zuloaga continued to serve as a deputy in the Cortes for many years after leaving office, holding various ministerial posts, including Minister of the Interior (1883-1884) and Minister of War (1886). He remained a staunch defender of conservative principles and the monarchy. In 1896, he was granted the title of *Marqués de Zuloaga* by Alfonso XIII, a recognition of his services to the crown. 

In 1900, he was appointed Director of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, following in his father’s footsteps.  He held this position until his death.  Zuloaga’s influence extended beyond politics; he was a patron of the arts and a collector of paintings.  He was a member of the Royal Spanish Academy, demonstrating his literary interests.  

Félix María Zuloaga died on January 7, 1911, in Madrid, at the age of 64. He was a central figure in the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy and the subsequent political development of Spain during a period of significant upheaval. His legacy remains complex, viewed by some as a pragmatic statesman who brought stability to a fractured nation, and by others as a conservative reactionary who stifled progressive reform.

title: Albert Outler
text:
Albert C. Outler was born on February 26, 1900, in Greenville, South Carolina, the son of William and Emma (Smith) Outler. His father was a Methodist minister, a profession that significantly shaped young Albert’s upbringing and instilled a lifelong commitment to religious scholarship. Outler’s early education followed his father’s itinerant ministry, attending schools in various South Carolina towns including Charleston and Spartanburg. He demonstrated early academic promise, particularly in languages and history. In 1916, he entered Wofford College in Spartanburg, a Methodist-affiliated institution, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1920, Phi Beta Kappa. 

Immediately following his undergraduate studies, Outler pursued theological education at Candler School of Theology at Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia, earning a Bachelor of Divinity degree in 1923. While at Candler, he was profoundly influenced by professors like George Wells Cook, a leading Methodist historian, and began to develop a scholarly interest in the theological writings of John Wesley, the founder of Methodism. He was ordained as a deacon in the Methodist Episcopal Church, South in 1922, and as an elder in 1924.

Outler’s early career involved pastoral work in South Carolina, serving as a minister at several churches between 1923 and 1930. However, his passion lay in academic pursuits. In 1930, he accepted a position as an instructor in Biblical Literature and Practical Theology at Scarritt College for Christian Workers in Kansas City, Missouri. This marked a turning point, leading to a distinguished career as a theological educator. 

In 1936, Outler moved to Perkins School of Theology at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas, where he would spend the next 36 years. He rose through the ranks, becoming a full professor of Theology in 1946 and serving as Dean of the School from 1951 to 1966. During his tenure as Dean, Perkins experienced significant growth in enrollment and academic reputation, establishing itself as a prominent theological center. 

Outler’s scholarship centered on the history of Christian thought, particularly the Wesleyan tradition. He became *the* leading 20th-century scholar of John Wesley. He meticulously researched, edited, and published the *Works of John Wesley*, a monumental 14-volume series published between 1974 and 1987 by Abingdon Press. This edition, based on original manuscripts and first editions, remains the standard scholarly resource for Wesley studies. Beyond the Wesley editions, Outler authored or edited over twenty books, including *John Wesley’s View of the Bible* (1964), *Theological Themes in John Wesley* (1974), and *John Wesley: A Biography* (1985). He also contributed extensively to theological journals and encyclopedias.

His commitment to ecumenical dialogue was also significant. He served on numerous committees and commissions for the Methodist Church and the broader ecumenical movement, including involvement with the National Council of Churches. He was a delegate to the 1968 and 1972 World Methodist Conferences. He was elected to the American Society of Church History in 1954.

Outler retired from Southern Methodist University in 1972, but continued to write and lecture extensively. He moved to a retirement community in Wilmore, Kentucky, near Asbury Theological Seminary, remaining active in the Wesleyan theological community. Albert Outler was married to Agnes Thompson in 1923, and they had two daughters, Elizabeth and Margaret. Agnes predeceased him in 1983. Albert Outler died on March 12, 1989, in Wilmore, Kentucky, at the age of 89. His legacy endures through his scholarship, his dedication to theological education, and his profound impact on the understanding of John Wesley and the Wesleyan tradition.

title: Gopi Sundar
text:
Gopi Sundar Govindan Nair, born November 28, 1977, in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India, is a prominent Indian film composer and singer known for his distinctive blend of electronic music, traditional Kerala instruments, and contemporary arrangements. His career spans over two decades, marked by innovative soundscapes and collaborations with leading figures in Malayalam cinema.

Gopi Sundar’s early life was steeped in music. His father, Govindan Nair, was a Carnatic vocalist and introduced him to classical music from a young age. He began learning Carnatic music at the age of four and later pursued a degree in music from the University of Kerala in Thiruvananthapuram. While formally trained in classical music, Gopi Sundar also developed a keen interest in Western musical styles, particularly electronic music. This fusion of influences would become a hallmark of his later work. He also holds a Bachelor of Technology degree in Electronics from College of Engineering, Thiruvananthapuram, showcasing his academic versatility. 

His professional journey began in 1999, initially working as a keyboard programmer in Chennai. He collaborated with several composers like A.R. Rahman, Harris Jayaraj, and Vidyasagar, honing his skills in sound design and arrangement. This experience proved invaluable in shaping his own musical identity. He contributed significantly to Rahman’s *Alaipayuthey* (2000) as a programmer.  He then moved to Dubai in 2001 where he worked independently for a few years before returning to India.

Gopi Sundar made his debut as an independent composer in Malayalam cinema with *Flash* in 2007, directed by Rony Mathew.  However, it was *Notebook* (2006) directed by Venu Nagavally that truly showcased his potential.  The album featured the popular song "Pattampoochi," sung by Vineeth Sreenivasan, which became a chartbuster. This marked the beginning of his successful collaboration with Vineeth, who also became a frequent lyricist in his films.  

Over the next few years, Gopi Sundar rapidly established himself as a leading composer in Malayalam cinema. *Poppins* (2008), directed by Venu Nagavally, further cemented his reputation. He composed scores for *Yodha* (2009), *Cocktail* (2010), *China Town* (2011), *Run Baby Run* (2012) and *Drishyam* (2013) - all commercially successful films. *Drishyam*, directed by Jeethu Joseph, won him the Kerala State Film Award for Best Music Director in 2013.  The songs "Dimaak Khara" and "Unne Nee Ennale" became hugely popular.  He also ventured into Tamil cinema in 2014 with *Idhu Enna Maayai*, directed by Sudha Kongara.

His most acclaimed work arguably came with *Bangalore Days* (2014), directed by Anjali Menon.  The soundtrack received widespread critical acclaim, featuring songs like "Njan Eesho", "Aarum Kayyarinje", and "Little Girl". It won him another Kerala State Film Award for Best Music Director in 2015.  He continued to deliver popular soundtracks in films like *Oru Vadakkan Selfie* (2015), *Paavada* (2016), *Jomonte Suvishesham* (2017), *Liger* (2017), *Aadhi* (2018) and *Lucia* (2019).  He also composed music for *Marakkar: Arabikadlinte Simham* (2021), directed by Priyadarshan, starring Mohanlal.  This epic historical drama featured a grand orchestral score.

Beyond film music, Gopi Sundar has also released independent albums and collaborated with several musicians. He has also sung numerous songs in his own compositions. His work often incorporates traditional Kerala instruments like the veena, chenda, and mridangam, blended seamlessly with electronic elements.  This unique approach has garnered him a devoted fan base.  He has composed over 200 songs in Malayalam and Tamil films.  He has also been involved in several live concerts and musical tours.  

In recent years, Gopi Sundar continues to be highly sought after in the Malayalam film industry, consistently delivering innovative and memorable soundtracks. He remains one of the most influential figures in contemporary Indian film music, celebrated for his ability to blend tradition with modernity in a uniquely captivating style.

title: Neil Googe
text:
Neil Googe, born on November 22, 1961, in Manchester, England, is a British computer scientist and internet pioneer best known as the creator of the world’s first web browser, WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion with the World Wide Web. His early life provided a foundation for this later innovation. He was the son of Bernard Googe, a physicist, and his mother was a teacher. From a young age, he displayed a precocious aptitude for mathematics and problem-solving, fostered by his father’s influence and a generally intellectually stimulating home environment. He attended Murgatroyd Hall, a prep school in Greater Manchester, before moving on to Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School, a selective state school in Hornchurch, Essex. 

Googe’s academic trajectory continued at the University of Lancaster, where he studied mathematics, graduating with a first-class honours degree in 1983. He then pursued doctoral research in artificial intelligence, specifically focusing on pattern recognition and machine learning, under the supervision of Professor David Hogg at Lancaster. This research involved developing systems capable of identifying patterns in complex data, a skill that would prove crucial in his later work. While completing his PhD, which he was awarded in 1986, Googe began to explore the possibilities of networked information systems.

The seeds of the WorldWideWeb were sown while Googe was working as a fellow at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva, Switzerland, from 1990 to 1994. CERN, famous for its particle physics research, also had a growing need for better information management amongst its globally distributed researchers. Existing systems, relying on disparate and incompatible formats, proved inadequate. Googe recognized the potential of hypertext – a concept explored by Vannevar Bush in the 1940s and Ted Nelson in the 1960s – to link information across different computers and platforms. 

In late 1990, Googe began developing a software program that would allow users to view and navigate hypertext documents on a network. Initially called WorldWideWeb, the software, written in C, combined features of a browser, a server, and an editor. It ran on a NeXT computer, a relatively obscure workstation favoured for its advanced graphical user interface. The first demonstration of WorldWideWeb took place on November 13, 1990, presented internally at CERN.  Crucially, the software allowed for not only text display but also images, creating the foundation for the multimedia web we know today. He also created the first web server, running on the same NeXT machine. 

Googe publicly released the WorldWideWeb software in August 1991, initially only available to other high-energy physics researchers.  This early version incorporated features like hypertext links, a universal resource identifier (URI) system, and the HTTP protocol – all fundamental elements of the modern web. Recognizing the potential for confusion with the broader concept of the "World Wide Web" itself, Googe renamed his software Nexus in 1994.  However, by this time, Tim Berners-Lee’s browser, also developed at CERN, had gained greater traction, aided by a more open licensing approach and strategic promotion.

Following his time at CERN, Googe returned to the UK and worked for several companies including Intergraph, and then in 1996 founded his own company, Applied Logic. He later co-founded, and became Chief Technology Officer of, Lodestone Systems, a company specializing in semantic web technologies, in 2001.  He remained with Lodestone until 2012.  In later years, Googe has been involved in consultancy work, focusing on semantic web and linked data technologies. 

While often overshadowed by Tim Berners-Lee, who is widely credited with inventing the World Wide Web, Googe’s contribution is significant.  He built the very first working software to access the web, demonstrating the feasibility of the concept and laying the technical groundwork for its future development.  He holds several patents related to web technologies, and continues to be recognized by the computing community as a pivotal figure in the history of the internet. He currently resides in the UK and continues to work in the field of computer science.

title: Henry VII of England
text:
Henry Tudor, later known as Henry VII, was born on January 28, 1457, at Pembroke Castle in Wales. His father, Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, was a distant relative of the English royal family through his mother, Margaret Beaufort, and a key supporter of Henry VI during the Wars of the Roses. His mother, Margaret Beaufort, was only thirteen years old at the time of his birth and a crucial figure in securing his future claim to the throne. Edmund Tudor died in November 1456, just three months before Henry's birth, leaving the young Henry as a precarious heir. 

Henry’s childhood was largely spent under the guardianship of his uncle, Jasper Tudor, Earl of Pembroke, who moved him between various estates in Wales and England to avoid the conflict between the Houses of York and Lancaster. The Yorkists, led by Edward IV, came to power in 1461, and Henry, being a Lancastrian, was constantly in danger. He received a humanist education, likely influenced by his mother’s piety and connections with scholars such as John Havyng. Following Edward IV’s death in 1483, his brother Richard III seized the throne, further complicating Henry’s position. 

In 1483, Henry fled to Brittany, France, under the protection of Duke Francis II. He spent the next fourteen years in exile, carefully cultivating alliances and planning his attempt to claim the English throne. He received financial support from his mother and explored potential marriage alliances to bolster his claim.  Crucially, he secured a promise of support from Charles VIII of France, although the assistance ultimately proved limited.

The death of Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on August 22, 1485, marked a turning point. Henry landed at Milford Haven in Wales with a small army of around 5,000 men, primarily French mercenaries and Welsh supporters. He defeated Richard III, ending the Wars of the Roses.  Richard III was the last Plantagenet king of England.  Henry, though his claim through his mother was somewhat tenuous, established his legitimacy by pledging to marry Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV, uniting the warring houses. 

Henry and Elizabeth married on January 18, 1486, at Westminster Abbey. This union, symbolized by the Tudor rose combining the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York, was instrumental in bringing stability to England.  Over his 23-year reign, Henry VII focused on consolidating royal power and restoring the finances of the crown. He established a new council, the Privy Council, to administer the country and curtailed the power of the nobility through laws like the Statute of Livery and Maintenance (1487), which restricted noblemen from maintaining armed retainers. 

Henry was a shrewd financial administrator.  He aggressively pursued those who had illegally obtained royal lands and imposed harsh penalties for rebellion, resulting in significant increases in royal revenue. He utilised legal mechanisms like the Court of Star Chamber to enforce law and order, often bypassing traditional legal processes.  During his reign, England’s revenue increased from approximately £12,000 to £26,000 annually. He also actively promoted trade and exploration, commissioning John Cabot to explore North America in 1497. 

Henry also pursued a cautious foreign policy, seeking to maintain peace with France and Scotland through diplomacy and strategic marriages. He signed the Treaty of Perpetual Peace with France in 1489, and his daughter Margaret married James IV of Scotland in 1503, attempting to create a lasting peace between the two nations. He built a strong navy, recognizing its importance for trade and defense. 

In later life, Henry became increasingly preoccupied with securing the succession. He faced challenges with the premature deaths of his first son, Arthur, Prince of Wales, in 1502, and his daughter Margaret. His second son, Henry, eventually succeeded him as Henry VIII.  Henry VII died on April 21, 1509, at Richmond Palace, Surrey. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, leaving behind a financially stable and politically secure England, setting the stage for the Tudor dynasty’s golden age.

title: Bif Naked
text:
Bethany “Bif” Lysaght, known professionally as Bif Naked, was born on April 26, 1970, in New Westminster, British Columbia, Canada. Her upbringing was marked by instability; her mother, a single parent, struggled with mental health issues and substance abuse, leading to a transient childhood spent moving frequently between foster homes and living on the streets of Vancouver beginning around age 13. This period of hardship profoundly shaped her worldview and later artistic expression. She adopted the nickname "Bif" – short for bifurcated, meaning divided – as a teenager, reflecting her feelings of being split between identities and experiences. She initially pursued poetry and spoken word performance as an outlet, participating in the Vancouver poetry slam scene in the early 1990s.

Bif's musical career began to take shape in 1996, when she started performing with a band initially called Bif and the Boom. The group quickly gained a local following in Vancouver, fueled by Naked’s dynamic stage presence and raw, emotionally honest lyrics. She signed with Sonic Records in 1997, and her debut album, *Bif Naked*, was released that same year. The album spawned the singles “Buggy” and “Lucky,” achieving significant airplay on Canadian radio and establishing her as a rising star. “Buggy” reached number 9 on the RPM Top Singles chart in Canada in 1997.

Her sophomore album, *I Bifiction*, released in 1998, further cemented her success. This record included the hit single “Champion,” which became an anthem for many and peaked at number 7 on the RPM Top 30 chart.  The album went platinum in Canada, selling over 100,000 copies.  She toured extensively throughout Canada and began gaining recognition internationally, opening for artists like Alanis Morissette and Sarah McLachlan.  Bif’s musical style blended alternative rock with elements of hip-hop, spoken word, and a distinctive, powerful vocal delivery. 

In 2000, Bif faced a significant health challenge when she was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 30. She underwent a lumpectomy, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, openly documenting her battle with the disease.  During her treatment, she continued to write and perform, releasing the EP *Moment of Truth* in 2001, which reflected her experiences.  She became a vocal advocate for breast cancer awareness and prevention, sharing her story to inspire others.  

Following her recovery, Bif released *Spidermilk* in 2002, an album that explored themes of resilience and healing.  She continued to release albums throughout the 2000s and 2010s, including *Deconstruction* (2003), *Vanilla Latte* (2006), *The Ruby Files* (2008), and *#MostBeautifulThings* (2014). While these later albums didn't reach the same commercial heights as her earlier work, they demonstrated her continued artistic evolution and willingness to experiment with different sounds.

Beyond music, Bif expanded her creative pursuits into acting, appearing in several Canadian television shows and films, including roles in *Da Vinci’s City Hall* (2005) and *The Strain* (2014-2017). She also authored a memoir, *I, Bif Naked*, published in 2010, detailing her tumultuous childhood, her battle with cancer, and her journey to self-acceptance. 

In recent years, Bif has remained active in the music scene, continuing to tour and record. She has also dedicated time to mentoring young artists and advocating for mental health awareness.  In 2023, she released a collaborative EP with DJ Starting Six titled *Bif Naked x Starting Six*.  She currently resides in Vancouver, where she continues to write, perform, and inspire audiences with her honest and unflinching artistry. Throughout her career, Bif Naked has received multiple Juno Award nominations, including a win for Best Alternative Album in 2000 for *I Bifiction*.

title: Danny Almonte
text:
Danny Almonte was born on February 24, 1989, in the Washington Heights neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City. His parents, Jose and Iris Almonte, were Dominican immigrants who instilled in him a strong work ethic and a passion for baseball from a young age. Growing up, Almonte displayed exceptional athletic ability, initially excelling in basketball, but his true calling became apparent as he began playing Little League baseball. He attended Public School 187 and quickly rose to prominence within the local youth leagues. 

Almonte's remarkable baseball journey truly took off with the Rolando Paulino Little League team in the summer of 2001. At just 12 years old, he became the focal point of the team’s improbable run to the Little League World Series championship.  The team, representing New York, was comprised largely of players from the Washington Heights area, a community facing economic hardship. Almonte, a powerfully built left-handed pitcher, was the team’s ace.  He pitched with a fastball that was clocked in the low-80s – an exceptionally high velocity for a player his age – and possessed an intimidating presence on the mound. 

During the Little League World Series in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, Almonte dominated the competition. He pitched three complete games, totaling 22 ⅓ innings, allowing only two runs and striking out 76 batters. His performance in the championship game against Aiea, Hawaii, on August 25, 2001, was particularly memorable. He pitched a complete-game shutout, allowing just one hit and striking out 16, leading Rolando Paulino to a 3-0 victory and the Little League World Series title. Almonte’s performance earned him national recognition and instant celebrity.  He appeared on television shows like "Good Morning America" and was featured in *Sports Illustrated*.

However, shortly after the team’s triumph, controversy erupted.  Documents surfaced indicating that Almonte was actually 14 years old, not 12 as required by Little League rules.  The age discrepancy was brought to light by a former league official, Carlos Velazquez, who alleged that Almonte’s father had provided falsified birth certificates.  Little League International conducted an investigation and, on September 11, 2001, officially stripped Rolando Paulino of its championship title.  The team was retroactively declared ineligible, and the runner-up, Aiea, Hawaii, was awarded the championship. 

The scandal cast a shadow over Almonte’s achievements. While he maintained he was unaware of any wrongdoing, the controversy significantly impacted his future baseball prospects. He attended Rice High School in Harlem, where he continued to play baseball, but the attention he received was often colored by the Little League controversy. He was drafted by the Tampa Bay Devil Rays in the 12th round of the 2007 Major League Baseball draft. 

Almonte spent several years in the minor league system, playing for teams like the Hudson Valley Renegades, Vero Beach Devil Rays, and Bowling Green Hot Rods. He never reached the major leagues, hampered by control issues and injuries. His highest level of play was with the Class A Bowling Green Hot Rods in 2009, where he posted a 5-7 record with a 4.68 ERA in 15 appearances. 

Following his baseball career, Almonte largely stayed out of the public eye. He briefly attended Borough of Manhattan Community College but did not complete a degree. He worked various jobs, including as a security guard and in construction.  In 2018, he was involved in a legal issue related to alleged involvement in a drug trafficking operation in New York City.  He was arrested and charged with conspiracy to possess and distribute controlled substances.  He ultimately pleaded guilty to a lesser charge in 2019 and received a sentence of probation. As of late 2023, Almonte continues to reside in the New York City area, attempting to rebuild his life and maintain a low profile. His story remains a cautionary tale about the pressures of youth sports and the consequences of dishonesty.

title: Diafra Sakho
text:
Diafra Sakho was born on November 24, 1989, in Thiès, Senegal. His early life was marked by a nomadic footballing journey across Europe before he eventually found a consistent foothold in professional football. Sakho didn’t begin his youth career in a formally structured academy system, instead initially playing for local Senegalese clubs before moving to France at the age of 15. He joined SC Bastia's youth setup in 2004, but spent only a short time there, before spells with several lower-league French clubs including AS Yzeure (2006-2007) and FC Villefranche Beaujolais (2007-2008). It was at Villefranche, playing in the Championnat de France amateur 2, that he began to attract attention with his goal-scoring prowess, netting 18 goals in 32 appearances during the 2008-2009 season.

This performance earned him a move to Valenciennes FC in Ligue 2 in the summer of 2009. Sakho spent two seasons with Valenciennes, gradually establishing himself as a key player. He made his professional debut on August 8, 2009, against Clermont Foot, and scored his first professional goal on November 20, 2009, against Tours. Over his time at the club, he contributed 16 goals in 64 league appearances. This form attracted the interest of larger clubs, and in July 2013, Sakho signed for West Ham United in the English Premier League for a reported fee of around £3.5 million.

Sakho made a significant impact upon arriving at West Ham. He scored on his Premier League debut on August 17, 2013, in a 2-0 win against Norwich City at Upton Park. He quickly became a fan favorite, forming a potent attacking partnership with fellow striker Andy Carroll. He finished his first season with 10 Premier League goals, becoming West Ham's top scorer for the 2013-14 campaign. A key moment of that season was his brace against Manchester United in December 2013, securing a memorable 3-1 victory for the Hammers.

The 2014-15 season saw Sakho continue to perform well, although hampered by injuries and international duty. He scored 8 Premier League goals despite missing a significant portion of the season. He also represented Senegal at the 2015 Africa Cup of Nations, where he scored a crucial goal against Ghana in the group stage.  He also dealt with a back injury which required specialist attention and affected his consistency. 

Sakho’s time at West Ham began to tail off after the 2015-16 season, with further injuries and the emergence of other attacking options limiting his playing time. In January 2018, he joined Ligue 1 side Rennes on loan for the remainder of the season, scoring 3 goals in 13 appearances. Upon his return to West Ham, he was released in July 2018.

He subsequently joined Turkish Süper Lig club Denizlispor in August 2018, signing a two-year contract. His time in Turkey was relatively short-lived, playing 28 times and scoring 8 goals before leaving in January 2020. Sakho then moved to Qatar, joining Al-Ahli SC in January 2020. He spent one season there, making 11 appearances and scoring 2 goals before the club was relegated.

In July 2021, Sakho returned to France, signing for Chamois Niortais, a Ligue 2 side.  He played for Niortais for two seasons, becoming a consistent performer, scoring 14 goals in 64 appearances.  He left the club in June 2023, becoming a free agent. In October 2023, he signed for Belgian Challenger Pro League side Patro Eisden, looking to continue his career in a new environment. 

Throughout his international career, Sakho earned 26 caps for Senegal between 2010 and 2018, scoring 6 goals and representing his nation at multiple Africa Cup of Nations tournaments. He retired from international football in 2018, focusing on club commitments.

title: Geraldo de Barros
text:
Geraldo de Barros was born on April 27, 1923, in São Paulo, Brazil, to Portuguese immigrant parents. His father, a photographer, instilled in him a fascination with the medium from a young age. While initially intending to study engineering, de Barros quickly gravitated towards visual arts, enrolling in 1943 at the Escola Nacional de Belas Artes (National School of Fine Arts) in Rio de Janeiro. However, he found the academic approach stifling and left after only a year, preferring a more self-directed path of artistic exploration. 

The mid-1940s were a period of intense artistic ferment in Brazil, and de Barros became a key figure in the Grupo Ruptura, founded in 1947. This group, consisting of artists like Waldemar Cordeiro, Luiz Sacilotto, and Ignácio de Loyola Brandão, explicitly rejected traditional Brazilian art forms and embraced a concrete, geometric aesthetic influenced by European Constructivism and Neo-Plasticism.  De Barros’s early work, though often photography, was fundamentally rooted in this concrete art philosophy. He wasn’t interested in photographic representation in a traditional sense; instead, he saw photography as a tool for exploring form, line, and spatial relationships. 

Between 1949 and 1951, de Barros held a significant role as art director for the advertising agency Companhia Brasileira de Publicidade (Brazilian Advertising Company). This experience, while providing financial stability, proved crucial to his artistic development. He began experimenting with photograms – images created without a camera, by placing objects directly onto photographic paper and exposing them to light.
