It was during his time at Loyola that his athletic talent began to emerge, initially in football, but he soon transitioned to track and field, specifically focusing on long-distance running. 

After completing his secondary education, Folorunsho secured a scholarship to study at the University of Iowa in the United States in 1949. He pursued a degree in Physical Education, graduating in 1953. This period was pivotal in his athletic development, as he benefited from world-class coaching and facilities. He quickly became a standout performer for the Iowa Hawkeyes track team, setting numerous university records. His training regime was rigorous, but he consistently displayed an exceptional level of discipline and determination.

Folorunsho’s international career began in 1952 when he represented Nigeria at the Helsinki Olympic Games in Finland. He competed in the 5,000 meters and the 10,000 meters, finishing 12th and 22nd respectively. While not securing a medal, his participation marked a significant moment for Nigerian athletics on the world stage. He followed this with a gold medal performance in the 6-mile run at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games held in Vancouver, Canada, clocking a time of 29 minutes and 40.8 seconds. This victory was particularly noteworthy as it was Nigeria’s first-ever gold medal at the Commonwealth Games.

He continued to represent Nigeria at subsequent international competitions. He competed at the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games, again in the 5,000m and 10,000m, but didn’t achieve the same level of success as in Helsinki. In 1958, he participated in the Cardiff Commonwealth Games, securing a silver medal in the 3-mile run with a time of 13 minutes and 59.4 seconds. Throughout his career, he consistently ranked among the top long-distance runners in the Commonwealth. He also held several national records in various distances, becoming a symbol of athletic excellence for Nigeria. 

Upon returning to Nigeria after completing his studies and competitive running career, Folorunsho dedicated himself to the development of sports within the country. He served as a sports administrator and educator for many years. He held positions within the Nigerian Amateur Athletic Association (NAAA) and the Ministry of Youth and Sports. He played a vital role in establishing and promoting sports programs at the grassroots level, focusing on identifying and nurturing young talent. He was instrumental in establishing physical education programs in schools across Nigeria, believing strongly in the importance of sports for youth development.

In 1976, he was appointed the Director of Sports Development in Nigeria, a position he held until his retirement in 1983. During his tenure, he oversaw significant improvements in sports infrastructure and training facilities. He actively campaigned for greater government investment in sports and advocated for the professionalization of athletes. 

Michael Folorunsho received numerous accolades for his contributions to sports. He was awarded the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) by the Nigerian government in 1963. He was also recognized by the University of Iowa, which inducted him into its Athletic Hall of Fame in 1982. He remained a respected figure in the Nigerian sporting community throughout his later life, often offering guidance and mentorship to younger athletes. Michael Folorunsho passed away on October 18, 1986, in Ile-Ife, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering athlete and a dedicated sports administrator. His achievements continue to inspire generations of Nigerian athletes.

title: Henryk Wieniawski
text:
Henryk Wieniawski was born on July 22, 1835, in Lublin, Congress Poland, which was then part of the Russian Empire. His father, Tadeusz Wieniawski, was a watchmaker who also possessed a strong passion for music and played the violin, and his mother, Regina, née Majewska, came from a family with musical inclinations. Recognizing his sons’ early aptitude, Tadeusz provided initial musical training to both Henryk and his younger brother, Józef, who also became a noted pianist and composer. Henryk’s first public performance occurred at the remarkably young age of seven, in Lublin, playing a concerto by Viotti. 

The family moved to Warsaw in 1843, where Henryk and Józef continued their studies. Henryk entered the Warsaw Conservatory in 1847, studying violin with Marjan Sawicki and composition with Apolinary Kątski. He demonstrated prodigious talent, completing the conservatory’s course in just three years, graduating in 1850. While still a student, he gained considerable attention performing solo concerts, even performing for the visiting Tsar Nicholas I in 1849.

Following his graduation, Wieniawski embarked on a European tour with Józef. They performed extensively throughout Russia, Germany, and France. In 1852, he began studies with the renowned violinist Camille Stamitz in Paris, further honing his technique. Paris became a crucial stepping stone in his career, and in 1853, he debuted at the Concerts Populaires, gaining favorable critical reception. This was followed by a successful performance at the prestigious Gewandhaus in Leipzig in 1854. 

Wieniawski’s reputation as a virtuoso rapidly grew. He toured extensively throughout Europe and the British Isles during the 1850s and 1860s, performing with leading orchestras and captivating audiences with his brilliant technique, expressive playing, and charismatic stage presence. He was particularly admired for his innovative use of harmonics, pizzicato, and left-hand techniques.  He was appointed the solo violinist to the Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna in St. Petersburg in 1860, a position he held until 1868. During this time, he frequently performed at the Russian Imperial Court.

His compositional output, though not as voluminous as his performance schedule allowed, is significant. He composed two violin concertos (in D minor, Op. 22, and in D major, Op. 28), a Polonaise Brillante No. 1 in D major, Op. 4, and No. 2 in A minor, Op. 24, a Fantasie Brillante on themes from Gounod's *Faust*, Op. 20, several mazurkas, scherzos, and other shorter pieces for violin and piano. His compositions are characterized by Polish folk influences, melodic invention, and technical demands that showcase the violin’s capabilities.

In 1873, Wieniawski accepted a professorship at the Brussels Conservatory, where he established a highly influential violin class. Among his notable students were Eugène Ysaÿe, Jacques Thibaud, and Zarathustra Pinchas.  He remained in Brussels for the rest of his life, continuing to perform and teach. 

In 1878, Wieniawski toured the United States, giving a series of highly acclaimed concerts.  He continued to tour periodically, but his health began to decline. He suffered from poor eyesight and a nervous ailment, which eventually led to a stroke. He died unexpectedly on August 3, 1880, in Brussels, Belgium, at the age of 45, while preparing for a concert tour. He was initially buried in Brussels, but his remains were later transferred to Warsaw in 1922 and interred in the Powązki Cemetery, a place of honor for Polish artists and intellectuals.

title: Naz Mitrou-Long
text:
Nazareth “Naz” Mitrou-Long was born on April 26, 1992, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, to Greek-Australian parents, Dimitri and Eleni Mitrou-Long. His father, Dimitri, was a professional basketball player himself, having played point guard for the York University Lions and briefly professionally in Australia. This familial connection to the sport profoundly shaped Naz’s early life, fostering a passion and dedication to basketball from a young age. He grew up in Mississauga, Ontario, and attended Father Michael Goetz Secondary School where he quickly established himself as a dominant force on the basketball court.

Mitrou-Long's impressive high school career garnered significant attention, averaging 37.6 points, 8.6 rebounds, and 4.9 assists in his senior year (2009-2010). He led Father Michael Goetz to a Region of Peel Athletic Association championship and earned numerous accolades, including being named a McDonald’s All-Canadian. Despite interest from several Canadian universities, Mitrou-Long chose to pursue his collegiate basketball career south of the border, accepting a scholarship to Iowa State University in Ames, Iowa, in 2010.

His time at Iowa State, playing for coach Fred Hoiberg, saw him develop into a versatile and impactful player. Initially a reserve, Mitrou-Long worked diligently to improve his game and earn playing time. He redshirted his first year (2010-2011) to further hone his skills. He then played four seasons (2011-2015), showcasing his scoring ability, particularly from beyond the three-point line, as well as his defensive tenacity. He finished his Iowa State career with 1,286 points, ranking 18th all-time in school history.  He averaged 15.9 points, 3.7 rebounds, and 2.8 assists in his senior season (2014-2015), earning him First Team All-Big 12 honors. He also was named the Big 12 Tournament MVP in 2014, leading the Cyclones to the tournament title.

Following his successful college career, Mitrou-Long went undrafted in the 2015 NBA draft. He immediately joined the Utah Jazz for the 2015 NBA Summer League, performing well enough to earn a non-guaranteed contract with the team. He appeared in 39 games for the Jazz during the 2015-2016 NBA season, averaging 5.3 points in 13.8 minutes per game. 

In July 2016, Mitrou-Long was waived by the Jazz and subsequently signed with the Philadelphia 76ers on a non-guaranteed contract. After a brief stint, he was cut before the start of the regular season. He then spent the 2016-2017 season bouncing between the Delaware 87ers (the 76ers’ G League affiliate) and short-term 10-day contracts with the Milwaukee Bucks and the New Orleans Pelicans, appearing in a total of 16 NBA games.

Seeking more stable playing time, Mitrou-Long moved to Europe in the summer of 2017, signing with Gran Canaria of the Spanish Liga ACB.  He enjoyed a successful two-year stint with the club, averaging 12.3 points in 44 games during the 2017-2018 season and 14.5 points in 31 games in the 2018-2019 season. Following Gran Canaria, he played for Turk Telekom Ankara in Turkey (2019-2020), averaging 16.4 points per game. 

In 2020, Mitrou-Long returned to Canada and joined the Scarborough Shooting Stars of the National Basketball League of Canada (NBLC). He led the league in scoring during the 2021 season, averaging 25.8 points per game and was named the NBLC Finals MVP after leading the Shooting Stars to the championship. He continued with Scarborough through the 2023 season, remaining a key player. 

In 2024, Mitrou-Long signed with the Newfoundland Growlers of the Canadian Elite Basketball League (CEBL), further continuing his professional career in Canada. Beyond his playing career, Mitrou-Long has been involved in basketball camps and clinics, giving back to the Canadian basketball community that nurtured his development. He remains a popular figure amongst Canadian basketball fans and a role model for aspiring players.

title: Blanca Errázuriz
text:
Blanca Errázuriz Richards, a prominent Chilean architect, was born in Santiago, Chile on February 28, 1928, into a family deeply rooted in Chilean history and politics. Her father, Jorge Errázuriz Alderete, was a lawyer and diplomat, and her mother, Blanca Richards Lyon, came from a family involved in mining. This background instilled in her a sense of social responsibility and a connection to the nation’s development which would heavily influence her professional life. She received her early education at the Liceo Javiera Carrera, a prestigious girls’ school in Santiago, and later entered the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile in 1946 to study architecture. 

Errázuriz was one of only three women in a class of over sixty students, facing considerable prejudice in a field largely dominated by men. She completed her degree in 1952, graduating with honors and receiving the prestigious Municipal Award for her final thesis project.  Immediately following graduation, she began working with the renowned architect Ricardo Tironi, a pivotal figure in the modernization of Chilean architecture and a proponent of integrating local materials and traditions. This apprenticeship, lasting until 1956, proved foundational to her developing design philosophy.

In 1956, Errázuriz established her own architectural practice, initially focusing on residential commissions. However, her career trajectory quickly expanded.  She became deeply involved in the national housing program initiated under President Jorge Alessandri Rodríguez in the early 1960s, known as the *Comité de Mejoramiento Urbano* (Committee for Urban Improvement). This program aimed to address the severe housing shortages in rapidly urbanizing Chile. Errázuriz didn't simply design houses; she pioneered a participatory approach, working directly with the future residents to understand their needs and integrate them into the design process. 

Her work during this period, particularly the *Villa San Rafael* in Peñalolén, Santiago (completed 1964), became a landmark example of socially conscious housing.  The project, encompassing 160 houses, was innovative for its use of prefabricated concrete panels – a cost-effective solution – and its emphasis on creating community spaces and fostering a sense of ownership amongst the residents.  It was significantly more than just providing shelter; she aimed to build neighborhoods.  

During the government of Salvador Allende (1970-1973), Errázuriz’s commitment to social housing intensified.  She served as Director of Housing and Urban Planning (SERVIU) for the Metropolitan Region of Santiago from 1971 to 1973.  In this role, she oversaw the construction of thousands of housing units, prioritizing affordable and dignified dwellings for the working class.  She also championed innovative financing mechanisms and community-based construction techniques. This period saw the initiation of several large-scale housing projects, including the *Unidad Vecinal El Volcán* in La Granja, which, though not fully completed due to the 1973 coup, remains a testament to her vision.

The military coup of September 11, 1973, profoundly impacted Errázuriz’s career. As a known supporter of the Allende government, she faced political persecution and professional marginalization. Her work on social housing was largely halted, and she was forced to navigate a restrictive political climate. Despite these challenges, she continued to practice architecture, often focusing on smaller-scale projects and renovations. 

In later life, Errázuriz dedicated herself to teaching and advocating for socially responsible architecture. She lectured at numerous universities in Chile and internationally, sharing her experiences and promoting the importance of community participation in urban planning.  She received numerous accolades for her contributions, including the National Prize for Architecture in 1992, the highest honor bestowed upon an architect in Chile. 

Blanca Errázuriz Richards died in Santiago, Chile on November 22, 2017, at the age of 89.  Her legacy endures not only through her built works but also through her enduring commitment to creating architecture that served the needs of the people and contributed to a more just and equitable society. She left behind a body of work that continues to inspire architects and urban planners committed to social responsibility.

title: Kion Smith
text:
Kion Smith, born on March 23, 1988, in Miami, Florida, was an American professional basketball player whose career, though relatively short-lived at the highest levels, was marked by impressive athleticism and a compelling personal story of overcoming significant adversity. He was the son of former NBA player and coach Kevin Smith and the brother of professional soccer player Klayton Smith. His early life was deeply intertwined with basketball, growing up around the game through his father’s career. Kevin Smith played for several NBA teams including the Miami Heat, Sacramento Kings, and Orlando Magic during the 1980s and 90s, and later coached in the NBA Development League. 

Kion Smith’s high school career took place at American Heritage High School in Plantation, Florida, where he quickly established himself as a standout player. He led the Patriots to a Florida Class 2A State Championship in 2006, averaging 23.4 points, 8.2 rebounds, and 3.1 assists per game during his senior year. He was named the 2006 Florida Class 2A Player of the Year and a McDonald's All-American, solidifying his status as a highly sought-after recruit. He finished his high school career with 1,803 points, a school record at the time.

He committed to the University of Florida, joining the Gators basketball program under coach Billy Donovan. Smith played for the Gators from 2006 to 2010. While he showed flashes of brilliance, his college career was hampered by a series of knee injuries. He suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his left knee during a practice in November 2007, causing him to miss the entire 2007-2008 season. He would later injure the same knee again, requiring further rehabilitation. Despite these setbacks, Smith managed to contribute significantly when healthy, showcasing his scoring ability and defensive prowess.  He finished his college career with 721 points over 88 games, averaging 8.2 points per game. 

Despite the injury concerns, Kion Smith was drafted by the Fort Wayne Mad Ants of the NBA Development League (now the NBA G League) in 2010. He had a brief stint with the Mad Ants before being called up to the NBA by the Cleveland Cavaliers on February 24, 2011, signing a 10-day contract. He played in three games for the Cavaliers, scoring a total of 9 points and grabbing 2 rebounds. Following the expiration of his contract, he was released by the Cavaliers.

He continued to bounce between the NBA G League and short stints with international teams. He played for the Iowa Energy (now the Iowa Wolves) in the 2011-2012 season, averaging 12.7 points per game in 34 appearances. He then spent time playing professionally in Turkey with Mersin Büyükşehir Belediyesi Spor Kulübü in 2012-2013, and later in South Korea with the Jeonju KCC Egis in the 2013-2014 season. Throughout these international experiences, he demonstrated his scoring abilities, often being a key offensive contributor for his teams.

However, the persistent knee injuries continued to plague his career, limiting his opportunities and impacting his performance. He attempted several comebacks, joining training camps with NBA teams, but was ultimately unable to secure another sustained position in the league.  

Kion Smith’s later life saw him transition away from professional basketball. Details regarding his post-basketball career have been kept relatively private. As of late 2023, he is involved in mentoring young basketball players, drawing on his experiences to guide them through the challenges of the sport. He resides in Florida and occasionally participates in basketball-related events. While his NBA career was brief, Kion Smith remains a respected figure in Florida basketball circles, remembered for his high school success, his resilience in the face of adversity, and his dedication to the game.

title: Ushoshi Sengupta
text:
Ushoshi Sengupta was born on November 22, 1989, in Kolkata, West Bengal, India, to Dr. Sudipto Sengupta, a physicist, and Dr. Chandrima Sengupta, a psychologist. From a young age, she demonstrated a keen interest in mathematics and logical reasoning, fostered by her parents’ academic environment. She received her primary and secondary education at South Point High School in Kolkata, consistently excelling in academic competitions, particularly in mathematics and science. Notably, she secured the first position in the West Bengal Joint Entrance Examination (WBJEE) in 2007 with a score of 99.995 percentile, a feat that garnered significant local media attention. 

Following her exceptional performance in the WBJEE, Sengupta enrolled in the Integrated M.Sc. – Ph.D. program in Theoretical Physics at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, in 2007. She quickly distinguished herself within the highly competitive academic environment, focusing her research on the field of string theory and quantum gravity. Her doctoral research, guided by Professor Rajesh Gomber, centered around exploring the AdS/CFT correspondence, a theoretical framework linking gravitational theories in anti-de Sitter space to conformal field theories. She completed her Ph.D. in 2013, at the remarkably young age of 23, with her thesis titled "Holographic aspects of strongly coupled systems."

Immediately after completing her doctorate, Sengupta pursued postdoctoral research at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada, from 2013 to 2016. During this period, she broadened her research interests to include black hole physics, information theory, and the quantum entanglement structure of spacetime. She collaborated with leading researchers like Robert Mann and collaborated on projects exploring the connection between entanglement and the emergence of spacetime geometry. 

In 2016, Sengupta joined the faculty at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kanpur as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Physics. She quickly established a thriving research group, mentoring several undergraduate and graduate students. Her research at IIT Kanpur continued to focus on the interplay between quantum information, gravity, and condensed matter physics. She was promoted to Associate Professor in 2022. 

Sengupta’s contributions to theoretical physics have been recognized through numerous awards and accolades. She received the INSPIRE Faculty Award from the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, in 2018, which supports promising young scientists.  She was awarded the Young Scientist Award from the Indian National Science Academy (INSA) in 2020 for her significant contributions to theoretical physics, particularly her work on holographic complexity and its relationship to black hole interiors. In 2023, she was selected as a Fellow of the Indian Academy of Sciences, Bangalore, a prestigious recognition of her scientific achievements.

Her research has resulted in over 60 peer-reviewed publications in leading scientific journals such as *Physical Review Letters*, *Journal of High Energy Physics*, and *Classical and Quantum Gravity*.  Her work has consistently garnered high citation counts, indicating its influence within the theoretical physics community.  She has also presented her research at numerous international conferences and workshops.

Beyond her research, Sengupta is actively involved in science outreach and education. She has delivered popular science lectures to high school students and participated in initiatives aimed at encouraging women in STEM fields.  She is also a member of various academic committees at IIT Kanpur and nationally, contributing to the development of science education and research policy. As of late 2023, Dr. Sengupta continues her research and teaching at IIT Kanpur, consistently pushing the boundaries of theoretical physics and mentoring the next generation of scientists.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Alonso Lara Ñiquen was born on February 23, 1923, in Puno, Peru, a city nestled high in the Andes near Lake Titicaca. His parents were both educators; his father, Braulio Lara Velásquez, was a schoolteacher and his mother, Carmen Ñiquen de Lara, also dedicated her life to education. This familial emphasis on learning significantly shaped his early life. He received his primary and secondary education in Puno, demonstrating a particular aptitude for mathematics and science. In 1942, he entered the National University of San Marcos in Lima, Peru, to study civil engineering. 

Lara’s university career was interrupted in 1945 when he joined the Peruvian Air Force, motivated by a desire to serve his country and a fascination with aviation. He trained as a pilot and specialized in aerial photography and surveying, skills that would prove invaluable in his later career. He graduated as a pilot officer in 1947, but continued his engineering studies concurrently, eventually earning his degree in civil engineering from San Marcos in 1951. He remained in the Air Force, rising through the ranks and gaining extensive experience in mapping and infrastructure projects, particularly in remote and challenging terrain.

In 1963, Lara transitioned from the Air Force to the Ministry of Public Works, beginning his full-time career in large-scale infrastructure development. He quickly gained recognition for his meticulous planning, efficient execution, and dedication to incorporating sustainable practices. His early projects focused on improving road networks in the Andean region, a critical need for connecting isolated communities. 

Lara’s most significant and internationally renowned achievement was the construction of the Carretera Marginal de la Selva, often referred to simply as the Marginal Highway. This ambitious project, initiated in 1965 and largely completed by 1978, involved building a 300-kilometer (approximately 186 miles) highway through the dense, humid rainforests of eastern Peru, linking several previously inaccessible towns and villages. The highway traversed incredibly difficult terrain, requiring innovative engineering solutions to overcome landslides, river crossings, and the challenging climate. Lara served as the project’s chief engineer and director, overseeing the entire operation. He prioritized employing local labor, providing employment and skills training to the communities along the route.  The project involved the construction of over 200 bridges and required the relocation of entire settlements in some cases, all handled with sensitivity and a commitment to minimizing disruption.

The Carretera Marginal de la Selva wasn't just a transportation artery; it facilitated economic development, access to healthcare and education, and improved the lives of thousands of people in the region. It remains a vital link to this day.  For his work on the highway, and his broader contributions to Peruvian infrastructure, Lara received numerous accolades, including the Order of the Sun of Peru, the nation’s highest honor, in 1980. He was also recognized internationally by engineering organizations. 

Beyond the Marginal Highway, Lara directed the construction of numerous other significant projects throughout his career, including irrigation systems, hydroelectric dams, and improved port facilities. He held various positions within the Ministry of Public Works, including Vice Minister, demonstrating his administrative capabilities alongside his technical expertise. He was known for his pragmatic approach, his commitment to quality, and his ability to manage complex projects within budget and on schedule.

Braulio Lara retired from public service in the late 1980s. He continued to consult on engineering projects and remained a vocal advocate for sustainable development and responsible infrastructure planning. He authored several technical papers and lectured at universities, sharing his knowledge and experience with future generations of engineers.  He spent his later years in Lima, dedicating time to his family and pursuing his passion for aviation. Braulio Alonso Lara Ñiquen passed away on July 18, 2017, in Lima, Peru, at the age of 94. His legacy remains firmly cemented as one of Peru’s most accomplished and impactful civil engineers, a builder who connected communities and fostered progress.

title: Rory Tapner
text:
Rory George Tapner was born on 22nd March 1960 in Nairobi, Kenya, to Brigadier John Tapner and his wife, Rosemary. His father served in the King’s African Rifles, and Rory’s early childhood was shaped by life in East Africa, attending the Duke of York School in Langata, Nairobi. This period instilled in him a strong connection to the natural world and a pragmatic, outdoorsy disposition. In 1972, the family relocated to England, settling in Gloucestershire, where Tapner completed his education at Cheltenham College, a boarding school with a strong tradition of rugby. He was a keen sportsman throughout his school years, demonstrating a particular aptitude for the game, and played for the school's 1st XV. 

Following school, Tapner embarked on a career in the City of London, joining Barings Bank in 1981 as a graduate trainee. He quickly proved himself a capable and insightful analyst, moving into the bank’s futures division. This was a period of significant growth and increasing complexity in financial markets, and Tapner thrived in the environment. He rose through the ranks, becoming a director in 1990 and subsequently managing director in 1994, responsible for overseeing Barings’ global options trading business. 

However, Tapner’s tenure at Barings is inextricably linked to the collapse of the bank in 1995, caused by the fraudulent trading activities of Nick Leeson in Singapore. While Tapner was not directly involved in Leeson’s actions, he was a key figure in the subsequent inquiry. He testified extensively before the Bank of England’s investigation, providing detailed accounts of the bank’s risk management procedures and the lack of oversight that allowed Leeson’s losses to escalate. The inquiry, led by Lord Justice Bingham, largely cleared Tapner of personal responsibility for the collapse, acknowledging his attempts to raise concerns about the Singapore operation. Nonetheless, the scandal cast a long shadow over his career.

After leaving Barings in the wake of its acquisition by ING in 1995, Tapner joined Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) in 1996, initially as a consultant before becoming head of European Equity Derivatives. He spent seven years at DMG, building a respected team and contributing to the bank’s expansion in the derivatives market. In 2003, he moved to Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB) as global head of equity derivatives, a position he held for five years. This role further solidified his reputation as a leading expert in the financial derivatives field, managing a substantial team and overseeing significant trading volumes.

In 2008, Tapner accepted the position of Chief Executive Officer of Turquoise, the pan-European multilateral trading facility (MTF) backed by the London Stock Exchange. He was tasked with establishing Turquoise as a viable competitor to established exchanges and dark pools. Under his leadership, Turquoise saw significant growth in trading volumes, particularly in complex derivative products. He successfully navigated the challenges of regulatory changes following the 2008 financial crisis, positioning Turquoise as a key player in the evolving European trading landscape. He stepped down from his role at Turquoise in December 2015.

Following his departure from Turquoise, Tapner became involved in several non-executive roles. He served as a non-executive director of MarketAxess Europe Ltd, a leading electronic trading platform, and as a member of the advisory board of several fintech companies. He also dedicated time to philanthropic pursuits, supporting conservation efforts in Africa, reflecting his early upbringing in Kenya. 

Rory Tapner currently resides in Gloucestershire, England. He remains a private individual, rarely granting interviews, but continues to be respected within the financial industry for his expertise and integrity. He is married to Sarah, and they have two children. He maintains a keen interest in rugby and continues to follow financial market developments closely.

title: Hayden Panettiere
text:
Hayden Lesley Panettiere was born on August 21, 1989, in Palisades, New York, to Lesley R. Vogel, a former soap opera actress, and Alan Lee “Skip” Panettiere, a fire captain. She has a younger brother, Jordan, also an actor. Her early childhood was spent moving frequently as her mother pursued acting roles and her father worked various jobs, including selling leather goods. By the age of four, Panettiere began appearing in commercials, including spots for P&G, Jell-O, and American Dairy Association. This early exposure led to her first television role in 1994, at the age of five, as Sarah Roberts in the soap opera *One Life to Live*, a part she played for four years until 1998. 

Following *One Life to Live*, Panettiere took on guest roles in various television shows, including *Law & Order*, *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit*, *ER*, and *Ally McBeal*. She had a recurring role as Lizzie Spaulding’s friend in *Guiding Light* from 1999 to 2000. A significant breakthrough came in 2000 when she landed the role of Zoey Brooks in the Disney Channel sitcom *Even Stevens*. The show, which aired until 2003, catapulted her to teenage stardom. She reprised her role as Zoey Brooks in the 2003 spin-off movie *The Even Stevens Movie*. 

While still starring in *Even Stevens*, Panettiere began to gain recognition in film. She voiced Kairi in the 2003 video game *Kingdom Hearts* and its sequels, a role she continued in subsequent installments. Her live-action film debut was in 1998’s *The Object of My Affection*, followed by roles in *Remember the Titans* (2000) and *Shanghai Noon* (2000). She gained further film prominence with *Bring It On: All or Nothing* (2003) and *Raising Helen* (2004).

The role that solidified Panettiere as a mainstream star was Claire Bennet, the cheerleader with regenerative abilities, in the NBC sci-fi drama *Heroes* (2006-2010). Her performance earned her Saturn Award nominations in 2007 and 2008, and she received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Supporting Actress – Series, Miniseries or Television Film in 2008. During this period, she also voiced Megara in Disney’s *Hercules* (2008) and starred in the horror film *Scream IV* (2011).

In the early 2010s, Panettiere continued to diversify her roles. She starred in the independent film *The Crazies* (2010), a remake of the 1973 George A. Romero film. She also began a relationship with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko, with whom she has a daughter, Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, born December 9, 2014.  She starred in the country music drama *Nashville* (2012-2018), playing aspiring country singer Juliette Barnes. Her musical performances on the show were critically well-received, and she released several original songs. 

However, Panettiere’s later life has been marked by struggles with postpartum depression and substance abuse. She publicly discussed her battle with postpartum depression following the birth of her daughter and entered treatment for substance abuse in 2015 and again in 2019. Her relationship with Klitschko ended in 2018, and a custody battle ensued regarding their daughter. In 2023, she entered a rehabilitation facility for eight months to address her struggles with alcohol and opioid addiction. 

Panettiere has been actively involved in animal rights activism, particularly concerning whaling. She has worked with the Whale and Dolphin Conservation organization and has spoken out against the practice of dolphin drive hunts in Japan, even being the subject of protests and controversy for her activism. While she has continued to take on occasional acting roles, including a recurring role in *Scream VI* (2023), her focus has increasingly been on her recovery and co-parenting her daughter.

title: Joseph Kony
text:
Joseph Kony was born in Odek, Uganda, in 1961, to a Catholic farmer, Lot Ajok, and his wife, Nora Otinga. He belonged to the Acholi ethnic group, a community that experienced marginalization following Uganda’s independence from Britain in 1962. Kony’s early life was relatively unremarkable; he attended the local Catholic primary school, St. Joseph’s College, but did not complete his education, reportedly leaving in the early 1980s. This period coincided with significant political instability in Uganda. Following the overthrow of Milton Obote in 1985, the National Resistance Army (NRA), led by Yoweri Museveni, gained power, further disenfranchising many Acholi, who had been heavily represented in the previous governments.

Kony’s entry into armed conflict began around 1986 with Alice Lakwena, a spirit medium who led a religious-millenarian rebellion known as the Holy Spirit Movement. Lakwena, claiming to be possessed by a spirit, attracted a large following amongst the Acholi, promising victory through spiritual power. Kony served as Lakwena’s bodyguard and military strategist, gaining valuable experience in guerrilla warfare. However, Lakwena’s movement was decisively defeated by the NRA in 1987, and she fled to South Sudan.

Following Lakwena's defeat, Kony formed the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) in 1987, initially presenting it as a movement to overthrow Museveni’s government and establish a state based on the Ten Commandments. However, the LRA quickly became notorious for its brutal tactics, far exceeding the scope of its stated religious or political aims. Kony blended Acholi traditional beliefs with distorted Christian theology, creating a cult of personality around himself. 

The LRA’s campaign of terror primarily targeted civilians in northern Uganda, but expanded to include parts of South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the Central African Republic. Between 1987 and 2006, the LRA abducted over 66,000 children, forcing them into service as soldiers and sex slaves. Boys were often brutally trained as child soldiers, compelled to participate in atrocities against their own communities, while girls were subjected to systematic sexual abuse and forced marriage to LRA commanders. The LRA is estimated to have killed over 100,000 people and displaced approximately 2 million during its reign of terror. 

Kony’s methods included widespread mutilation, such as the cutting off of lips and ears, as a form of psychological warfare and control. He employed a complex command structure based on a mixture of loyalty and fear, utilizing former abductees to maintain control over his forces.  

Numerous attempts were made to negotiate with Kony. In 2006, peace talks began in Juba, South Sudan, mediated by the government of Southern Sudan, but stalled repeatedly due to Kony’s unwillingness to sign a final peace agreement and his insistence on amnesties for war crimes.  

International attention intensified in 2012 with the viral video "Kony 2012" produced by the organization Invisible Children, which aimed to raise awareness and pressure the U.S. government to increase its involvement in capturing Kony. While the campaign generated significant awareness, it also drew criticism for its oversimplification of the conflict and its financial practices.

In late 2008, a joint military operation involving the Ugandan People’s Defence Force (UPDF), the South Sudanese army, and the Congolese army, codenamed "Operation Lightning Thunder," forced the LRA out of Uganda and into the dense jungles of the Central African Republic.  

Despite decades of pursuit, Joseph Kony remains at large.  He is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on 33 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, issued in 2005.  While the LRA has significantly diminished in strength, with numbers estimated at a few hundred fighters, sporadic attacks continue in remote areas of the CAR, South Sudan, and the DRC.  Kony’s current whereabouts are unknown, but he is believed to be hiding in the remote, lawless regions of the Central African Republic.

title: Noel Malicdem
text:
Noel Malicdem was born on November 22, 1946, in Manila, Philippines, to Vicente Malicdem, a lawyer, and Dolores Villanueva-Malicdem, a teacher. He was the eldest of four children. His early education took place at the Ateneo de Manila High School, where he graduated as valedictorian in 1964. This academic success foreshadowed a consistently strong performance throughout his life. He then pursued a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration degree at the Ateneo de Manila University, completing it in 1968, again graduating with honors – *magna cum laude*.  

Immediately following his undergraduate studies, Malicdem traveled to the United States to further his education. He enrolled at the Harvard Business School, earning a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree in 1972.  His time at Harvard was pivotal, exposing him to modern management techniques and a global business perspective. Upon completion of his MBA, he was offered a position at Procter & Gamble (P&G) in Cincinnati, Ohio. 

Malicdem’s career at P&G spanned over two decades, beginning as an Assistant Marketing Manager in 1972. He rapidly ascended through the ranks, demonstrating a talent for brand building and strategic leadership.  He held various positions, including Marketing Manager for Pampers diapers, Brand Manager for Tide laundry detergent, and eventually, Country Manager for P&G Philippines in 1987.  During his tenure as Country Manager, P&G Philippines experienced significant growth, with sales increasing by an estimated 30% within three years, largely attributed to his innovative marketing campaigns and strengthened distribution networks. He was known for focusing on consumer understanding and tailoring products to the specific needs of the Philippine market.

In 1993, Malicdem left P&G to embark on a new chapter as the President and Chief Operating Officer of Ayala Land, Inc., the real estate arm of the Ayala Corporation, one of the oldest and largest conglomerates in the Philippines.  This marked a significant shift from consumer goods to property development. He quickly proved his adaptability and leadership capabilities in this new sector. Under his leadership, Ayala Land underwent a period of rapid expansion and diversification. He spearheaded the development of large-scale, integrated, mixed-use projects, including the Bonifacio Global City (BGC) in Taguig, Metro Manila, which began substantial development during his time. BGC, a former military base, transformed under his guidance into a premier financial and lifestyle district. 

Malicdem held the position of President and COO of Ayala Land from 1993 to 2006. In 2006, he was appointed Chairman of the Board, a position he held until his retirement in 2011.  During his time as Chairman, Ayala Land continued its expansion, launching new projects and solidifying its position as the leading property developer in the Philippines. He was instrumental in the company’s consistent financial performance, overseeing a period where Ayala Land’s market capitalization grew to over ₱100 billion (approximately $2.2 billion USD at the time of his retirement).

Beyond his corporate roles, Malicdem was actively involved in various civic and professional organizations. He served as a Trustee of the Ateneo de Manila University and the Philippine Business for Social Progress. He also held positions in several industry associations, advocating for responsible business practices and sustainable development. He was a recipient of numerous awards and recognitions throughout his career, including the Management Man of the Year award from the Management Association of the Philippines in 2005.

Following his retirement from Ayala Land in 2011, Malicdem remained active as a consultant and advisor to various businesses. He dedicated more time to philanthropic endeavors, focusing on education and community development. He passed away on February 15, 2023, in Manila, at the age of 76, after a prolonged illness. He is survived by his wife, Corazon “Cora” de la Cruz-Malicdem, and their three children, Maria Cristina, Vicente Rafael, and Antonio Miguel. His legacy is remembered as a visionary leader who significantly contributed to the growth and development of both the consumer goods and real estate industries in the Philippines.

title: Maja Jager
text:
Maja Jager, born Maria Johanna Jager on December 21, 1938, in Cologne, Germany, was a pioneering computer scientist whose work significantly advanced the field of compiler construction and program optimization. Her early life was deeply impacted by the devastation of World War II. Her father, Wilhelm Jager, was a professor of electrical engineering at the University of Cologne, and her mother, Elisabeth Jager (née Lueders), was a mathematics teacher. The university was heavily damaged during the war, and the family faced considerable hardship in the postwar years. This environment instilled in Maja a pragmatic and resourceful approach to problem-solving, qualities that would define her academic career.

She began her formal education in Cologne, attending the Mädchengymnasium (girls’ grammar school) until 1957. Following her Abitur (high school diploma), she enrolled at the University of Cologne, initially studying mathematics and physics. However, she quickly gravitated towards the nascent field of computer science, recognizing its potential. She completed her Diplom (Master's degree equivalent) in mathematics in 1962, focusing on numerical mathematics.  Her thesis, supervised by Professor Heinrich Soeffing, explored methods for solving systems of linear equations.

In 1963, Jager moved to the United States to pursue doctoral studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She joined the Computation Structures Group, led by Professor Harold Stone, a key figure in compiler design. She earned her PhD in Computer Science in 1967 with a dissertation titled “Optimization of Object Code.” This work laid the foundation for much of her subsequent research and established her as a leading figure in the optimization of machine code. 

Her PhD research focused on techniques for improving the efficiency of code generated by compilers. At the time, compilers were often seen as a bottleneck in the performance of computer programs. Jager developed innovative methods to reduce code size and execution time, specifically targeting the IBM System/360 architecture. Her work involved analyzing the structure of object code and applying transformations to eliminate redundancies and improve instruction scheduling. 

Following her PhD, Jager accepted a position at the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC) in 1967, becoming one of the first women appointed to the faculty in the Computer Science department. She remained at UCSC for her entire career, achieving the rank of Professor Emerita. At UCSC, she continued to refine and expand her work on compiler optimization, becoming particularly renowned for her research on global code optimization, register allocation, and instruction selection. 

A significant achievement was her development of the “Liveness Analysis” algorithm, a fundamental technique used in compiler optimization to determine which variables are in use at any given point in a program. This algorithm, published in a series of influential papers throughout the 1970s and 80s, became a cornerstone of modern compiler technology and is still widely used today.  She collaborated extensively with other researchers, including Ronald Cytron, on extending and applying liveness analysis.

Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Jager's research shifted towards parallel processing and software pipelining, techniques aimed at exploiting the potential of multi-processor systems. She explored how to optimize code for execution on parallel architectures, addressing challenges related to data dependencies and communication overhead.  She also contributed to the development of tools and methodologies for analyzing the performance of parallel programs.

Maja Jager was a dedicated educator, mentoring numerous graduate students who went on to successful careers in academia and industry. She was known for her rigorous standards and her commitment to fostering independent thinking. She was a member of the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and served on the editorial boards of several leading computer science journals. 

Maja Jager passed away on October 27, 2023, in Santa Cruz, California, at the age of 84. Her contributions to compiler optimization remain profoundly influential, and her work continues to shape the way computers execute software today. She never married and had no children, dedicating her life to her academic pursuits and leaving a lasting legacy in the field of computer science.

title: Wil Nieves
text:
Wil Nieves was born Wilfredo Nieves on March 26, 1976, in Carolina, Puerto Rico. He grew up in a baseball-centric household; his father, Wilfredo Nieves Sr., was a professional baseball player who spent several seasons in the minor leagues, primarily as a catcher. This early exposure profoundly influenced young Wil, who quickly developed a passion for the game, mirroring his father’s position behind the plate. He attended Colegio Angelicum in Carolina, but his athletic talent quickly overshadowed his academic pursuits.

Nieves was drafted by the Colorado Rockies in the third round of the 1994 Major League Baseball draft, with the 87th overall pick. He was scouted by Ray Poitevent, who recognized his potential as a defensive catcher with a strong arm. He began his professional career with the Asheville Tourists, a Rockies’ short-season A affiliate, in 1994, hitting .235 in 48 games. He steadily progressed through the Rockies’ farm system, playing for the Bend Rockies (1995), New Haven Skyhawks (1996-1997), and Colorado Springs Sky Sox (1998-1999). 

Nieves made his Major League debut with the Colorado Rockies on May 20, 1999, as a late-inning defensive replacement for Jeff Reed. He appeared in 22 games for the Rockies that season, batting .200 with one home run and 7 RBIs. While not a power hitter, Nieves quickly established himself as a reliable defensive catcher, known for his game-calling ability and strong throwing arm. He spent the next two seasons (2000-2001) primarily with Colorado Springs, seeing limited action in the majors.

In November 2001, Nieves was traded to the San Francisco Giants for reliever Aaron Fultz. This trade proved pivotal for his career. He spent the 2002 season as a backup catcher for the Giants, backing up Brent Mayne, and then became the primary catcher in 2003 after Mayne was traded. He had a solid year in 2003, playing in 124 games and hitting .268 with 6 home runs and 49 RBIs. 

He continued as the Giants’ starting catcher through 2005, becoming a fan favorite for his consistent defense and quiet leadership. However, his offensive numbers remained modest. In 2006, he was again traded, this time to the Washington Nationals for outfielder Jose Guillen. 

Nieves spent two seasons with the Nationals (2006-2007), again serving as a starting catcher. He was then traded to the Chicago White Sox in January 2008, where he spent a single season, primarily backing up A.J. Pierzynski. His final major league stint was with the Milwaukee Brewers in 2009, appearing in just 26 games before being released in July.  Over his 10-year Major League career, Nieves played in 784 games, accumulating a career batting average of .245 with 28 home runs and 241 RBIs. He recorded a .991 fielding percentage as a catcher, with 59 passed balls and 141 runners caught stealing.

Following his retirement as a player, Nieves transitioned into coaching. He began as a volunteer coach at his alma mater, Colegio Angelicum, in Puerto Rico. In 2012, he joined the Chicago Cubs organization as a coach for the Boise Hawks, a short-season A affiliate.  He progressively moved up through the Cubs’ minor league system, becoming the manager of the South Bend Cubs (Class A) in 2015 and the Tennessee Smokies (Double-A) in 2017. 

In November 2018, Nieves was named the Major League bullpen coach for the Chicago Cubs under manager Joe Maddon. He held that position until 2020. In January 2021, he was hired as the bullpen coach for the San Francisco Giants, returning to the organization where he had previously enjoyed success as a player. As of late 2023, he continues to serve as the bullpen coach for the Giants, contributing his extensive knowledge and experience to the team's pitching staff. He resides in Puerto Rico with his family during the offseason, remaining actively involved in baseball development programs for young players on the island.

title: Tom Buk-Swienty
text:
Tom Buk-Swienty, born Tomasz Buk-Swienty on November 29, 1947, in Warsaw, Poland, was a highly influential and prolific record producer, best known for his work with Motown artists during the 1980s and 90s. His early life was marked by displacement and a deep connection to music. His father, a Polish diplomat, and his mother, a classical pianist, fled Poland with young Tomasz in 1949, seeking political asylum in the United Kingdom following the communist takeover. They eventually settled in London, where Buk-Swienty received his education, attending Holland Park School. 

His musical journey began as a teenager, initially playing drums in various bands. He quickly gravitated towards the technical aspects of music, demonstrating a keen ear and an aptitude for recording and mixing. In the mid-1960s, he secured a position as a junior engineer at Olympic Studios in Barnes, London, a renowned facility that hosted acts like The Rolling Stones, The Who, and Jimi Hendrix. This apprenticeship proved invaluable, exposing him to top-tier musicians and recording techniques. He rose through the ranks at Olympic, becoming a fully-fledged engineer by 1969. 

A pivotal moment came in 1974 when he accepted an invitation from Berry Gordy, the founder of Motown Records, to relocate to Los Angeles and work at Motown's West Coast recording facilities. Gordy was seeking to revitalize the label’s sound and recognized Buk-Swienty’s potential. Initially employed as a staff engineer, Buk-Swienty quickly became a key figure in Motown’s production team. He worked on projects with established artists like Diana Ross, The Jackson 5, Marvin Gaye, and Stevie Wonder, learning the nuances of the “Motown Sound” while simultaneously contributing his own evolving style.

The 1980s marked Buk-Swienty’s ascent to producer. He began co-producing with established names and then took the helm on full projects. He is particularly celebrated for his work with Lionel Richie, co-producing and engineering the massively successful album *Can't Slow Down* (1983), which sold over 10 million copies and won a Grammy Award for Album of the Year. He followed this with *Dancing on the Ceiling* (1986), another multi-platinum success for Richie.

Beyond Richie, Buk-Swienty’s production credits read like a who’s who of 1980s and 90s pop, R&B, and rock. He produced albums for Bob Seger, including *Like a Rock* (1986) which featured the title track that became a cultural touchstone, and Rod Stewart's *Out of Order* (1988), which reached number one in the UK. He also worked extensively with Barbra Streisand, producing her albums *Till I Loved You* (1988) and *Back to Broadway* (1993). He also notably produced albums for Johnny Mathis, Patti LaBelle, and Kenny Rogers. His production style was characterized by a meticulous attention to detail, a focus on strong vocal performances, and a blend of traditional instrumentation with emerging technologies like synthesizers and drum machines. 

Throughout his career, Buk-Swienty earned numerous accolades, including multiple Grammy Awards and platinum and gold records. He was known for his quiet professionalism and his ability to foster a collaborative environment in the studio. He also maintained a relatively low public profile, preferring to let the music speak for itself. 

In the late 1990s, Buk-Swienty began to scale back his work, though he continued to produce occasionally. He resided in Los Angeles with his wife, Mary. He passed away on December 25, 2023, at the age of 76, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most successful and respected record producers of his generation. His contributions to popular music remain significant, shaping the sound of the 80s and 90s and influencing countless artists.

title: Asafa Powell
text:
Asafa Powell, born November 23, 1982, in Spanish Town, Jamaica, is a retired Jamaican sprinter widely regarded as one of the greatest 100-meter runners of all time. His early life was marked by a natural athletic ability, honed initially through football and cricket before his high school coach, Fitz Coleman, recognized his exceptional speed at Charlemont High School. Coleman steered him towards track and field, and Powell quickly demonstrated potential, reaching the final of the 100m at the 1999 CARIFTA Games, though he didn’t medal. 

Powell’s breakthrough came in 2004. After attending the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) on a track scholarship, he returned to Jamaica and began to consistently lower his personal best. On June 5th, 2005, at the Grand Prix in Modena, Italy, he officially entered the elite ranks by clocking 9.99 seconds, becoming the third Jamaican to break the 10-second barrier, following Don Quarrie and Michael Frater.  He continued his ascent throughout the year, winning gold in the 100m at the 2005 World Championships in Helsinki, Finland, with a time of 9.87 seconds.  This marked his first major international championship victory.

The following year, 2006, was arguably the pinnacle of Powell’s career. He embarked on a remarkable streak, breaking the world record in the 100m not once, but twice. On June 3rd, in Gateshead, England, he ran 9.84 seconds, eclipsing Justin Gatlin’s previous mark.  Just over a month later, on July 15th, in Rieti, Italy, he further lowered the record to 9.77 seconds, a time that stood for three years. Throughout 2006, he won 18 of 19 races, cementing his status as the dominant force in sprinting. He also secured a Commonwealth Games gold medal in Melbourne, Australia, running 10.03 seconds.

Despite his consistent speed and dominance, Olympic gold proved elusive. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, he was considered a strong favourite, but suffered a hamstring injury during the trials and finished fifth in the final with a time of 9.95 seconds.  The gold medal went to Usain Bolt, signaling a shift in the landscape of men’s sprinting. Powell continued to compete at a high level, focusing on the 100m and occasionally the 4x100m relay. 

In 2009, he was part of the Jamaican 4x100m relay team that set a new world record of 37.31 seconds at the World Championships in Berlin, alongside Nesta Carter, Michael Frater, and Usain Bolt. However, this record was later revoked in 2017 due to Carter’s subsequent doping violation.  He won a silver medal in the 100m at the 2009 World Championships, finishing behind Usain Bolt with a time of 9.82 seconds. 

Powell faced adversity in 2013 when he tested positive for the banned stimulant oxilofrine. He initially received an 18-month ban, later reduced to six months on appeal due to mitigating circumstances relating to a contaminated supplement. He returned to competition in 2014, but never regained his previous form. 

He continued to compete sporadically, aiming for another Olympic appearance, and was part of the Jamaican team at the 2016 Rio Olympics, though he did not reach the final.  He also participated in the 2017 World Championships in London. He officially announced his retirement from competitive sprinting in November 2022, at the age of 40. 

Throughout his career, Asafa Powell achieved 94 sub-10 second 100m runs, a testament to his consistency and speed – a record that remains unchallenged. He holds the distinction of being the first man to legally break the 10-second barrier multiple times.  He is a national hero in Jamaica, celebrated for his contributions to the country’s rich sprinting tradition and his positive impact on aspiring athletes.  Following retirement, Powell has focused on business ventures and motivational speaking, remaining a prominent figure in the world of athletics.

title: Cleopatra
text:
Cleopatra VII Philopator, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, was born in Alexandria in 69 BCE. She was a member of the Macedonian Greek dynasty founded by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great, who took control of Egypt after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE. Cleopatra’s father was Ptolemy XII Auletes, and her mother’s identity is debated, though most scholars believe it was likely Cleopatra V Tryphaena, his sister. She had three siblings: Ptolemy XIII, Arsinoe IV, and Ptolemy XIV.

Cleopatra received a comprehensive education, unusually for women of her time, learning multiple languages including Egyptian – a skill that distinguished her from most of her predecessors who primarily spoke Greek. This ability to converse directly with Egyptian priests and dignitaries fostered a stronger connection with the native population.  She also studied mathematics, philosophy, diplomacy, and astronomy.  

Ptolemy XII died in 51 BCE, naming Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIII as joint rulers.  Almost immediately, conflict arose between the siblings. Ptolemy XIII, influenced by his advisors, particularly the eunuch Pothinus, moved to oust Cleopatra. By 48 BCE, she had been forced to flee Alexandria and raise an army in Syria.  

This internal struggle coincided with the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great. Pompey arrived in Egypt seeking refuge after his defeat at the Battle of Pharsus in 48 BCE, but was assassinated by Ptolemy XIII’s advisors, hoping to gain favour with Caesar. Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BCE and, becoming embroiled in the Egyptian succession dispute, favoured Cleopatra.  Legend recounts she had herself smuggled into Caesar’s presence, rolled in a carpet, to appeal to him directly.  

Caesar sided with Cleopatra, defeating Ptolemy XIII’s forces in a series of battles, culminating in the Battle of the Nile in 47 BCE, where Ptolemy XIII drowned. Cleopatra was restored to the throne, and she co-ruled with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV.  In 47 BCE, she gave birth to Ptolemy Caesar, known as Caesarion, widely believed to be Caesar’s son.  

Caesar and Cleopatra spent several months together in Egypt before Caesar left in 47 BCE to deal with further conflicts in the Roman world. She followed him to Rome in 46 BCE with Caesarion, residing in one of his villas. Caesar’s assassination on March 15, 44 BCE, forced Cleopatra to return to Egypt. Ptolemy XIV died shortly after, likely poisoned by Cleopatra, allowing her to install Caesarion as her co-ruler.

Following Caesar's death, the Roman world was again thrown into turmoil, this time between Mark Antony, Octavian (Caesar’s adopted son), and Lepidus, forming the Second Triumvirate.  Antony summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus in 41 BCE to answer questions about her loyalty.  She arrived in a lavish display of wealth and power, captivating Antony.  

Antony and Cleopatra began a romantic and political alliance. They spent the winter of 41-40 BCE in Alexandria, and she bore him three children: twins Cleopatra Selene II and Alexander Helios in 40 BCE, and Ptolemy Philadelphus in 36 BCE.  Antony’s political decisions increasingly favoured Cleopatra and her children, including granting them territories in the eastern Mediterranean. This, coupled with his public displays of affection for Cleopatra and his divorce from Octavian’s sister Octavia, enraged Octavian.

The escalating tensions culminated in the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.  Antony and Cleopatra’s combined naval forces were decisively defeated by Octavian’s fleet.  They retreated to Egypt, where Octavian pursued them.  

In 30 BCE, with Octavian’s forces closing in on Alexandria, Antony, falsely believing Cleopatra to be dead, fell on his sword.  Cleopatra, after attempting negotiations with Octavian, committed suicide, traditionally believed to be by allowing an asp (Egyptian cobra) to bite her, on August 12, 30 BCE.  She was 39 years old.  Caesarion was executed on Octavian’s orders shortly after. Egypt became a Roman province, marking the end of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the final chapter of ancient Egyptian independence.

title: Rachel Weisz
text:
Rachel Hannah Weisz was born on March 7, 1970, in Westminster, London, England, to David Weisz, an inventor, and Catherine (née Samers), a teacher. Her father was born in Vienna, Austria, a Jewish refugee fleeing Nazi persecution, while her mother is of English and Italian ancestry. Weisz spent her early childhood in Hampstead, North London, and at the age of 14, she and her family moved to Cambridge when her father took a position at the University. This relocation proved pivotal, as she attended Cambridge Arts and Sciences Sixth Form and later, St. John's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1991 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English Literature. 

During her time at Cambridge, Weisz’s interest in acting developed. She co-founded the amateur Cambridge Footlights dramatic club, following in the footsteps of notable alumni like Emma Thompson and Stephen Fry. While there, she performed in several productions, including a production of ‘Design for Living’ that caught the eye of agent Jane Hewland. After graduating, Weisz initially considered a career in law or journalism, but ultimately decided to pursue acting professionally, starting with small roles in television.

Her early television work included appearances in ‘Inspector Morse’ (1993) and ‘The Scarlet Pimpernel’ (1999). Her film debut came in 1994 with a minor role in ‘Death Machine’. She gained wider recognition with a supporting role in the independent film ‘Gas Land’ (1995), and further solidified her presence with roles in ‘Sense and Sensibility’ (1995), where she played Miss Pickering, and ‘Stealing Beauty’ (1996), directed by Bernardo Bertolucci. 

The late 1990s and early 2000s saw Weisz taking on increasingly diverse and challenging roles. She garnered critical acclaim for her performance in ‘The Mummy’ (1999) and its sequel, ‘The Mummy Returns’ (2001), becoming a commercially successful action star while simultaneously seeking out independent projects. A significant turning point came in 2005 when she won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Tessa Quayle in Fernando Meirelles’s ‘The Constant Gardener’, alongside Ralph Fiennes. This win cemented her status as a respected dramatic actress.

Following her Oscar win, Weisz continued to choose roles that showcased her range. She starred in ‘Proof’ (2005), a stage adaptation of David Auburn’s play, receiving a Tony Award nomination for her performance. Further film roles included ‘Eragon’ (2006), ‘Youth’ (2007), ‘The Lovely Bones’ (2009), and ‘Dream House’ (2011). 

In 2011, she began a relationship with Daniel Craig, whom she married in a private ceremony in New York City on June 22, 2011. The couple have a daughter, born in 2018. Weisz also has a son, Henry Aramis Knight, born in 1996, from a previous relationship with director Sam Mendes, whom she was with from 1998 to 2010. 

Weisz’s career continued to thrive in the 2010s and 2020s. She received further critical acclaim for her roles in ‘The Favourite’ (2018), earning her a BAFTA Award and another Academy Award nomination, and ‘Disobedience’ (2017). More recent work includes ‘Black Widow’ (2021), reprising her role as Melina Vostokoff from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and ‘Dead Ringers’ (2023), a psychological thriller series for Apple TV+, where she plays both Beverly and Chad Mantle. 

Throughout her career, Rachel Weisz has consistently balanced mainstream and independent films, showcasing her versatility and commitment to challenging roles. She has received numerous awards and nominations, establishing herself as one of the most respected and accomplished actresses of her generation. Her filmography boasts over 50 film credits, alongside her stage and television work, demonstrating a sustained and impressive career spanning over three decades.

title: Gretl Braun
text:
Margarete “Gretl” Braun was born on November 3, 1915, in Munich, Bavaria, Germany, the younger sister of Eva Braun, who would later become the wife of Adolf Hitler. Her parents were Friedrich Braun, a schoolteacher, and Franziska “Fanny” Heylmann. Gretl’s early life was relatively conventional for a middle-class Bavarian girl. She attended the state-run Lyzeum in Munich, graduating in 1934. Unlike her sister Eva, who dropped out of school to work as a photographer and secretary, Gretl completed her education and enrolled at the Higher Professional School for Physical Education in 1934, aiming to become a physical education teacher. 

Gretl excelled in sports, particularly gymnastics and fencing, demonstrating a natural athleticism. She successfully completed her studies in 1938 and subsequently secured a position as a physical education teacher at the state girls’ school in Munich. This career path allowed her a degree of independence and normalcy, even as her sister’s life became increasingly intertwined with the Nazi regime. While Eva Braun’s relationship with Hitler was known within a close circle, Gretl initially maintained a more distant relationship with the Führer, though she inevitably became a frequent visitor to his various headquarters.

In 1938, Gretl began a relationship with SS-Gruppenführer Hermann Fegelein, who was a member of Hitler's personal staff and later became the liaison officer between Hitler and Himmler. Their courtship was protracted and complicated. Hitler initially disapproved of the relationship, viewing Fegelein as insufficiently aristocratic and fearing the potential for gossip. He demanded Fegelein serve on the front lines during World War II as a test of his loyalty and bravery. Fegelein served with distinction, earning the Knight’s Cross of the Iron Cross in 1943, and Hitler eventually relented. 

Gretl and Hermann Fegelein were married on June 3, 1944, in a lavish ceremony at Schloss Ritterschwaigen, a hunting lodge near Munich. The wedding was attended by high-ranking Nazi officials including Hitler, Heinrich Himmler, Hermann Göring, and Martin Bormann, serving as witnesses. Hitler himself gave Gretl away. The marriage was reportedly a happy one, though shadowed by the circumstances of their lives. 

As the war drew to a close, Gretl and Hermann followed Hitler to the Führerbunker in Berlin in April 1945. Fegelein was tasked with organizing the defense of the bunker and attempting to establish communication with the outside world. On April 28, 1945, Fegelein was arrested by Hitler after being accused of attempting to escape the bunker with a large sum of money and forging documents. Hitler ordered his execution, and Fegelein was shot by SS officers in the garden of the Reich Chancellery. The exact reasons for his arrest and execution remain somewhat debated, with theories ranging from genuine attempted desertion to a power struggle orchestrated by rival SS figures.

Following her husband’s execution, Gretl remained in the bunker.  She was present during Hitler's suicide on April 30, 1945, and witnessed Eva Braun’s death shortly thereafter.  She attempted to escape Berlin with a group including Hitler’s personal physician, Ludwig Stumpfegger, and Eva Braun’s dentist, Hugo Blaschke, but they were captured by Soviet troops on May 1, 1945, near the Potsdamer Platz. Stumpfegger and Blaschke died shortly after capture, likely from suicide.

Gretl Braun was interrogated by the Soviets and held as a prisoner of war for over three years. She was initially held in various Soviet camps, including one in Pankracy Prison in Warsaw. She provided information about life in the bunker and the final days of Hitler, though the extent to which her testimony was considered reliable is debated. She was eventually released on December 22, 1948. 

After her release, Gretl Braun lived a quiet and reclusive life. She worked as a shop assistant in a chocolate shop in Munich and later as a caretaker. She never remarried and rarely spoke about her experiences during the war. She died on December 19, 1987, in Steinebach, Bavaria, at the age of 72. She was buried next to her husband, Hermann Fegelein.

title: Esteban Espíndola
text:
Esteban Espíndola was born on December 12, 1942, in San Juan del Río, Querétaro, Mexico. His parents, Alejandro Espíndola and María de la Luz Vargas, were both educators, fostering an environment that valued learning and intellectual curiosity from a young age. San Juan del Río, a historically significant city with a strong artistic tradition, likely influenced his early aesthetic sensibilities. He began formal art training at the age of 14, enrolling in the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Querétaro in 1956. This foundational period focused on classical painting techniques, laying the groundwork for his later explorations in abstraction. 

In 1962, Espíndola moved to Mexico City to continue his education at the prestigious Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas (ENAP) of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL). There, he studied under prominent Mexican artists like José Luis Cuevas and Luis Ortiz, figures who were pushing the boundaries of traditional Mexican art. This exposure proved pivotal, steering him away from purely representational work and towards a more conceptual and abstract approach. He completed his studies at ENAP in 1966, earning a degree in painting and sculpture.

The late 1960s and 1970s marked a period of significant artistic development for Espíndola. He became involved with the Ruptura group, a collective of young artists challenging the dominance of muralism and seeking new forms of expression. Ruptura, founded in 1968, advocated for a more international and conceptual art scene in Mexico, and Espíndola’s work increasingly reflected this ethos.  During this time, he experimented extensively with geometric abstraction, hard-edge painting, and minimalist sculpture, often utilizing industrial materials like steel and aluminum. His early exhibitions, notably a group show at the Galería Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City in 1970, showcased these new directions.

Throughout the 1980s, Espíndola's style evolved to incorporate more organic forms and a richer color palette, although the underlying principles of geometric abstraction remained central. He began to explore the relationship between art and architecture, creating site-specific installations and public sculptures. A particularly notable commission came in 1985, when he was selected to create a large-scale public sculpture for the Plaza Galerías Guadalajara, a prominent shopping center in Guadalajara, Jalisco. The sculpture, a complex arrangement of steel forms titled “Estructura Dinámica,” became a landmark and remains in place today. 

Espíndola’s work gained international recognition through numerous solo and group exhibitions. He exhibited at the Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City on several occasions, including a retrospective of his work in 1992. He also participated in important international events, such as the 1988 São Paulo Biennial in Brazil and the 1991 Venice Biennale in Italy.  He held solo exhibitions in cities across the United States, including New York, Los Angeles, and Houston, and his work was acquired by major collections, including the Museo Nacional de Arte Moderno (MAM) in Mexico City, the Museo de Arte de Querétaro, and various corporate collections. 

Beyond his artistic practice, Espíndola dedicated a significant portion of his life to education. He served as a professor at the ENAP from 1978 until his retirement in 2012, mentoring generations of young artists. He was known for his rigorous approach to teaching and his commitment to fostering critical thinking and experimentation.  

Esteban Espíndola passed away on January 27, 2018, in Mexico City at the age of 75, following a prolonged illness. He left behind a substantial body of work that continues to be exhibited and studied, solidifying his position as one of Mexico’s most important abstract artists. His legacy rests not only on the visual impact of his sculptures and paintings but also on his dedication to teaching and his influence on the development of contemporary art in Mexico.

title: Josiah Maduabuchi
text:
Josiah Maduabuchi, often referred to as “Joe Maduabuchi,” was a pioneering Nigerian electrical engineer and entrepreneur, instrumental in establishing and developing the television broadcasting industry in Nigeria. He was born on October 28, 1935, in Umuezeala, Ehime Mbano Local Government Area, Imo State, Nigeria, to parents Elijah and Martha Maduabuchi. His early education took place at the Church Missionary Society (CMS) Primary School, Umuezeala, from 1943 to 1949, followed by secondary education at Dennis Memorial Grammar School, Onitsha, between 1950 and 1954. He distinguished himself as a bright student, demonstrating a particular aptitude for mathematics and science.

In 1955, Maduabuchi received a scholarship to study Electrical Engineering at the University of Manchester, England. He completed his Bachelor of Science degree in 1959, becoming one of the first Nigerian engineers to graduate from a British university with such a qualification. This was a significant achievement in a period when access to higher education for Nigerians was limited. Following graduation, he briefly worked with the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) in London, gaining practical experience in television broadcasting technology. 

Returning to Nigeria in 1960, coinciding with the nation’s independence, Maduabuchi joined the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation (NBC), later renamed the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria (FRCN). He was assigned to the newly established television service, WNTV (Western Nigeria Television), in Ibadan.  Here, he played a crucial role in the installation and commissioning of the station’s first television transmitter, a 60kW transmitter purchased from Marconi in the United Kingdom. This was a landmark achievement, marking the beginning of television broadcasting in Nigeria and West Africa.

Maduabuchi wasn’t simply an installer; he quickly became a central figure in the technical operations of WNTV. He was responsible for maintaining the station’s equipment, training local staff, and adapting broadcasting techniques to the Nigerian context.  He also actively participated in the planning and execution of outside broadcasts, covering important national events like the 1963 Federal Elections and the visit of Queen Elizabeth II in 1966.  His expertise was vital during a period when skilled technical personnel were scarce.

In 1968, recognizing a gap in the market for indigenous technical expertise in broadcasting, Maduabuchi established his own company, Maduabuchi Communications Limited. This company quickly became a leading provider of broadcast engineering services in Nigeria, undertaking projects for both government and private broadcasters.  He secured a major contract in 1973 to install and commission the first colour television transmitter for the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) Channel 5 in Lagos, again utilizing Marconi equipment.  

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, Maduabuchi Communications expanded, handling projects involving the installation of television transmitters, studio equipment, and satellite earth stations across Nigeria. He was instrumental in the establishment of several state-owned television stations and played a key role in the expansion of NTA’s national coverage.  His company employed and trained a significant number of Nigerian engineers and technicians, contributing significantly to the development of local capacity in the broadcasting sector.
